title: Developmental anatomy — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: Obeng's HB2 embryology lectures (F. K. Addai, SMD KNUST)

questions.stem: The complete process of spermatogenesis, from spermatogonium to spermatozoon, takes about
questions.why: Human spermatogenesis requires several cycles of seminiferous epithelial development, progressing through spermatogonial proliferation, meiosis and spermiogenesis. Approximately 64 days is one conventional estimate; other references estimate around 74 days, depending on methodology.

notes.B: Sixteen days approximates one seminiferous epithelial cycle in classical human estimates, rather than the entire spermatogenic process.
notes.C: Twenty-four days is a conventional estimate for a component of germ-cell development, rather than the entire sequence from spermatogonium.
notes.D: Seven days is insufficient for the multiple proliferative, meiotic and differentiation stages needed to produce mature-shaped testicular spermatozoa.
notes.E: Ninety days exceeds the conventional intratesticular estimate and may conflate spermatogenesis with additional post-testicular transport and maturation time.

questions.stem: Spermiogenesis, the cytodifferentiation of a spermatid into a spermatozoon, takes about
questions.why: Spermiogenesis is the final nondividing differentiation of haploid spermatids, involving acrosome formation, nuclear condensation, flagellar assembly and removal of excess cytoplasm. Approximately 24 days is a conventional teaching estimate, rather than an invariant duration.

notes.A: Forty-eight days substantially exceeds the conventional duration assigned specifically to the final morphological differentiation of spermatids.
notes.C: Sixty-four days is a conventional estimate for complete spermatogenesis, including earlier proliferation and meiosis as well as spermiogenesis.
notes.D: Sixteen days approximates one human seminiferous epithelial cycle in classical descriptions, rather than the stated conventional spermiogenesis duration.
notes.E: Two days is too short to represent the usual extended sequence of spermatid morphological and organelle remodelling.

questions.stem: The blood-testis barrier, formed by tight junctions between Sertoli cells, separates a basal compartment (spermatogonia, mitosis) from an adluminal compartment where
questions.why: Sertoli-cell tight junctions divide seminiferous epithelium into basal and adluminal compartments. Developing spermatocytes cross this barrier and undergo most meiotic development in the protected adluminal environment, which also contains differentiating spermatids.

notes.A: Testosterone is produced predominantly by Leydig cells in the interstitial tissue outside the seminiferous epithelial barrier.
notes.B: Leydig cells occupy testicular interstitial connective tissue rather than the adluminal compartment of seminiferous tubules.
notes.D: Spermatogonial mitoses occur principally within the basal compartment, before differentiating germ cells progress across Sertoli junctions.
notes.E: Spermatozoa are released into the tubular lumen and stored mainly in epididymal regions, rather than the adluminal compartment.

questions.stem: Meiosis in the male occurs only after puberty, which is important because meiotic products
questions.why: Meiotic cells carry novel antigens; the blood-testis barrier plus post-pubertal timing (mature immune system) prevents autoimmune destruction and infertility.

questions.stem: The reserve stem cell of the spermatogenic lineage that can continue spermatogenesis throughout life is the
questions.why: In the traditional human spermatogonial classification, dark type A spermatogonia are regarded as a relatively quiescent reserve population, while pale type A cells contribute to active renewal. Modern stem-cell models recognise greater functional complexity.

notes.A: Type A pale spermatogonia are conventionally regarded as the more actively proliferating population rather than the relatively quiescent reserve.
notes.B: Type B spermatogonia are differentiating mitotic precursors committed towards spermatocyte development, rather than the traditional reserve stem-cell population.
notes.C: Primary spermatocytes enter meiosis I and are more differentiated than the spermatogonial populations maintaining germ-cell production.
notes.D: Secondary spermatocytes are short-lived haploid products of meiosis I and do not constitute a self-renewing reserve stem-cell population.

questions.stem: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division at which stage, from fetal life until puberty?
questions.why: Primary oocytes enter meiosis during fetal development and arrest in the prolonged diplotene, or dictyotene, stage of prophase I. Selected oocytes resume meiosis near ovulation after puberty, while others can remain arrested for decades.

notes.B: Diplotene belongs to prophase I; meiosis II does not contain the prolonged fetal dictyotene arrest described here.
notes.C: Metaphase II is the usual arrest stage of the ovulated secondary oocyte, rather than the fetal primary oocyte.
notes.D: Anaphase I involves separation of homologous chromosomes after meiotic resumption, not the prolonged primary-oocyte arrest stage.
notes.E: Interphase precedes or separates cell division stages; the arrested primary oocyte has already entered prophase of meiosis I.

questions.stem: Meiotic arrest of the primary oocyte is maintained by oocyte maturation inhibitor secreted by the
questions.why: Follicular (granulosa) cells secrete oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI), holding the oocyte in meiotic arrest.

questions.stem: A normal ejaculate volume is about
questions.why: Ejaculate volume varies with abstinence interval, collection completeness and individual physiology. The stated 1.8–5.5 mL range is a plausible conventional teaching range, but volume alone cannot determine fertility and clinical reference limits differ.

notes.A: Six to nine millilitres is above the central conventional teaching range, although individual ejaculates may exceed typical volumes.
notes.B: Twenty millilitres is substantially greater than ordinary ejaculate volumes and is not the typical reference range.
notes.D: Volumes below half a millilitre are substantially lower than the conventional typical range and may warrant contextual assessment.
notes.E: Ten to fifteen millilitres exceeds ordinary central ejaculate volume estimates, rather than representing the usual physiological range.

questions.stem: For fertility, at least what fraction of spermatozoa should be motile with progressive forward movement?
questions.why: At least ~40% of sperm should be motile with forward progression; a minimum of ~15 million per ejaculate is needed.

questions.stem: Immotile sperm flagella due to a ciliary (dynein) defect, as in Kartagener's syndrome, is
questions.why: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener's) gives immotile flagella and infertility.

questions.stem: The term for a complete absence of spermatozoa in the ejaculate, even after centrifugation, is
questions.why: Azoospermia denotes absence of spermatozoa from ejaculated semen, including examination of an appropriately centrifuged sample. It can result from impaired sperm production or obstruction of sperm transport despite the presence of seminal fluid.

notes.B: Aspermia denotes absence of ejaculate or semen emission, rather than semen being present but containing no detectable sperm.
notes.C: Oligozoospermia describes reduced sperm concentration, with spermatozoa still detectable rather than completely absent from semen.
notes.D: Asthenozoospermia describes reduced sperm motility rather than the complete absence of spermatozoa from an examined ejaculate.
notes.E: Teratozoospermia refers to a reduced proportion of morphologically normal sperm rather than the absence of detectable sperm.

questions.stem: During the acrosome reaction, the enzyme that digests the cumulus/corona cells around the oocyte is
questions.why: Hyaluronidase digests the corona radiata; acrosin (exposed on the inner acrosomal membrane) helps penetrate the zona; neuraminidase is also released.

questions.stem: Fertilization proceeds in three sequential steps: penetration of the corona radiata, penetration of the zona pellucida, and

options.label: C
options.text: fusion of the oocyte and sperm cell membranes

questions.why: Fertilisation conventionally involves sperm passage through the cumulus and corona radiata, traversal of the zona pellucida and fusion with the oocyte plasma membrane. Fusion triggers oocyte activation and subsequent pronuclear development.

notes.A: Oocyte meiosis II normally finishes after fertilisation-associated activation rather than being completed before ovulation and sperm contact.
notes.B: Decidualisation involves maternal endometrial stromal differentiation and is not the membrane interaction completing the conventional fertilisation sequence.
notes.D: The first cleavage occurs after fertilisation and zygote formation, rather than completing sperm interaction with the oocyte membrane.
notes.E: Morula formation follows repeated cleavage divisions and therefore occurs considerably later than sperm–oocyte membrane fusion.

questions.stem: Polyspermic fertilization in the human characteristically

options.label: B
options.text: is the usual mechanism of twinning

options.label: D
options.text: dies at or after the 8-cell stage

questions.why: A polyspermic pre-embryo does not proceed beyond a few cleavages and dies around the 8-cell stage.

questions.stem: A hydatidiform mole, with masses of trophoblast secreting large amounts of hCG and no viable fetus, may arise from

options.label: C
options.text: arrest of the oocyte in dictyotene

questions.why: Loss of a pronucleus (often with polyspermic fertilization) gives molar pregnancy with excess trophoblast and hCG.

questions.stem: Cleavage of the human zygote is described as holoblastic, meaning the division furrows

options.label: A
options.text: pass completely through the whole cell

options.label: B
options.text: involve only part of the cell

questions.why: Holoblastic cleavage means that cytokinetic furrows divide the entire zygote or blastomere into separate daughter cells. In humans, early cleavage partitions existing cytoplasm into progressively smaller blastomeres without substantial overall embryonic growth.

notes.B: Partial cleavage is termed meroblastic and occurs in some yolk-rich eggs, rather than normal human complete cleavage.
notes.C: Early cleavage redistributes existing cytoplasm rather than adding substantial new cytoplasmic volume during each successive division.
notes.D: Human cleavage begins within the uterine tube before blastocyst formation and implantation, rather than only after endometrial attachment.
notes.E: Successive blastomeres generally become smaller during early cleavage because the original cytoplasmic volume is partitioned among increasing cell numbers.

questions.stem: The ball of blastomeres is moved from the oviduct to the uterus by peristalsis and by

options.label: B
options.text: a ciliary escalator of oviductal cilia

questions.why: Tubal cilia beat towards the uterus while coordinated smooth-muscle contractions assist transport of the early conceptus. Together these mechanisms move the developing cleavage-stage embryo through the uterine tube towards the uterine cavity.

notes.A: Uterine suction is not the conventional principal transport mechanism; tubal ciliary activity and muscle contractions provide coordinated movement.
notes.C: Human blastomeres lack locomotor flagella and depend on maternal reproductive tract transport mechanisms to reach the uterus.
notes.D: Blastomeres undergo cleavage and compaction but do not propel the whole conceptus through coordinated muscular contractions.
notes.E: Gravity alone cannot explain directional tubal transport, which relies on active ciliary movement and smooth-muscle activity.

questions.stem: Compaction of the morula is driven mainly by
questions.why: Compaction involves increased E-cadherin-mediated adhesion between blastomeres, producing tighter cell contacts and changes in cell shape. Outer cells acquire apical polarity, helping establish differences between inner and outer cell populations before blastocyst formation.

notes.A: Human chorionic gonadotropin is principally associated with trophoblastic endocrine activity during implantation and does not drive initial morula compaction.
notes.B: Sonic hedgehog regulates later developmental patterning rather than providing the principal adhesion mechanism tightening contacts between blastomeres.
notes.D: The zona pellucida persists during compaction and is shed later during blastocyst hatching before successful implantation.
notes.E: Sodium–potassium ATPase helps establish osmotic gradients during blastocoel formation, rather than mediating the initial cell adhesion of compaction.

questions.stem: The blastocoel cavity forms when outer trophoblast cells pump ions using
questions.why: Polarised trophectoderm cells use sodium–potassium ATPase and associated ion transport to generate an osmotic gradient favouring fluid accumulation inside the embryo. Tight junctions retain this fluid, allowing formation and expansion of the blastocoel.

notes.A: Sodium–glucose cotransport may support cellular metabolism, but sodium–potassium ATPase provides the characteristic ion gradient driving blastocoel expansion.
notes.B: Aquaporins facilitate water movement, but they require an osmotic driving force generated by ion transport rather than pumping water independently.
notes.C: Chloride shift describes erythrocyte bicarbonate–chloride exchange during carbon dioxide transport, not the principal mechanism of blastocoel cavity formation.
notes.E: Hydrogen–potassium ATPase is associated with gastric acid secretion and is not the characteristic pump driving blastocyst cavity expansion.

questions.stem: In the morula-to-blastocyst transition, trophoblast fate in the outer cells is promoted by the transcription factor
questions.why: CDX2 supports trophectoderm identity in the classical mammalian lineage model. Outer-cell polarity and Hippo pathway regulation influence nuclear YAP–TEAD activity and trophectoderm-associated gene expression, although human lineage timing differs from mouse development.

notes.A: NANOG is associated principally with pluripotent epiblast identity rather than the classical transcriptional programme promoting outer trophectoderm fate.
notes.B: OCT4 supports pluripotency-related programmes and is not the conventional principal trophectoderm-promoting transcription factor specified in this question.
notes.C: SOX17 is associated particularly with primitive endoderm and later endodermal differentiation rather than the classical outer trophectoderm programme.
notes.D: NODAL participates in developmental signalling and lineage specification but is not the transcription factor classically associated with trophectoderm identity.

questions.stem: Pluripotency of the inner cell mass is maintained by the transcription factors
questions.why: OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG form a core regulatory network supporting pluripotency, particularly in the emerging epiblast within the inner cell mass. Their interactions maintain developmental potential and help distinguish pluripotent from extraembryonic cell programmes.

notes.B: CDX2 and YAP contribute to trophectoderm-associated programmes, while GATA6 is associated with primitive endoderm rather than core pluripotency.
notes.C: SOX17 and GATA6 support primitive endoderm differentiation, while CDX2 is associated with trophectoderm rather than the core pluripotency network.
notes.D: NODAL, WNT3 and FGF8 participate in developmental signalling and patterning, rather than constituting the canonical core pluripotency transcription-factor trio.
notes.E: Snail regulates epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, while SHH and BMP mediate developmental signalling rather than forming the core pluripotency transcriptional network.

questions.stem: Implantation requires a receptive endometrium and a blastocyst that has

options.label: B
options.text: hatched out of the zona pellucida

questions.why: The expanding blastocyst must escape the surrounding zona pellucida so its trophectoderm can directly contact receptive endometrial epithelium. Hatching permits subsequent apposition, adhesion and invasion during the appropriate endometrial implantation window.

notes.A: Gastrulation occurs after implantation has begun and therefore is not required before the blastocyst can attach to endometrium.
notes.C: Retention of the zona pellucida physically separates trophectoderm from endometrial epithelium and generally prevents normal implantation-associated adhesion.
notes.D: The three embryonic germ layers arise during gastrulation after early implantation, rather than being required for initial attachment.
notes.E: Early endometrial receptivity depends largely on maternal luteal progesterone; blastocyst hatching rather than embryonic progesterone secretion enables direct attachment.

questions.stem: The three stages of implantation, in order, are
questions.why: Implantation conventionally begins with apposition, a relatively loose alignment of blastocyst and receptive endometrium. Adhesion strengthens trophoblastic attachment, after which invasive trophoblastic cells penetrate the endometrial epithelium and underlying maternal tissue.

notes.A: Stable adhesion normally precedes invasion, so placing invasion before adhesion reverses the later stages of the conventional sequence.
notes.B: Apposition is the initial loose contact and must precede the firmer adhesive and invasive interactions with maternal tissue.
notes.D: Adhesion follows initial apposition, rather than occurring before the blastocyst first aligns with receptive endometrial epithelium.
notes.E: Invasion follows establishment of contact and attachment, rather than preceding both apposition and adhesion during normal implantation.

questions.stem: The usual site of implantation is the

options.label: E
options.text: lower uterine segment over the os

questions.why: Normal implantation occurs within the endometrium of the uterine body, commonly near the fundus on its anterior or posterior wall. This location supports subsequent placental development and differs from ectopic or abnormally low implantation.

notes.A: The ampulla is the common fertilisation site, but implantation there constitutes a tubal ectopic pregnancy rather than normal implantation.
notes.B: Implantation on the ovarian surface represents ovarian ectopic pregnancy rather than the normal uterine endometrial implantation site.
notes.C: Cervical implantation is an abnormal ectopic pregnancy location and is not the usual site supporting normal placental development.
notes.E: Low implantation near the internal cervical os can lead to placenta praevia rather than the usual upper uterine location.

questions.stem: Monochorionic-diamniotic (Mo-Di) monozygotic twins, sharing one placenta but with separate amnions, make up about
questions.why: Most monozygotic twin pregnancies are monochorionic diamniotic, conventionally estimated at approximately two thirds. A shared chorionic placenta creates potential vascular anastomoses, while separate amniotic sacs distinguish this arrangement from monoamniotic twinning.

notes.A: Five percent is closer to conventional estimates for monoamniotic twins, not the common diamniotic pattern.
notes.B: Thirty percent is closer to the conventional proportion of dichorionic diamniotic monozygotic twin pregnancies.
notes.C: Monozygotic twins may have different chorionic arrangements, so they do not all share one placenta.
notes.D: One percent of all twins uses a different denominator and substantially understates this common monozygotic arrangement.

questions.stem: Monochorionic-monoamniotic (Mo-Mo) twins, the riskiest type, carry a mortality of about
questions.why: Mo-Mo twins (~5% of twins) share one placenta and one amnion, with a mortality around 20%.

questions.stem: Conjoined twinning is possible only in which type of monozygotic twins?
questions.why: Conjoining results from late (post-bilaminar-disc) splitting and occurs only in Mo-Mo twins.

questions.stem: Conjoined twins joined at the cranium are termed
questions.why: Craniopagus describes conjoined twins united at the skull, with variable sharing of cranial tissues and vessels. Anatomical classification identifies the principal union site rather than necessarily specifying all shared organs.

notes.A: Pygopagus describes union near the sacral or buttock region rather than at the cranium.
notes.B: Parapagus describes side-by-side union involving varying portions of the trunk rather than isolated cranial union.
notes.D: Thoracopagus describes union at the thorax and may involve shared cardiac structures rather than skull attachment.
notes.E: Omphalopagus describes union around the abdominal or umbilical region rather than the cranial vault.

questions.stem: The simultaneous presence of two embryos conceived weeks apart in the same uterus is
questions.why: Superfetation denotes conception of an additional embryo during an established pregnancy, requiring unusual persistence or resumption of reproductive processes. It differs from superfecundation, in which separate ova from the same cycle are fertilised.

notes.A: Mosaicism describes genetically distinct cell populations originating from one zygote, not temporally separated conceptions.
notes.B: Chimerism describes genetically distinct cell populations from different zygotes within an individual rather than successive pregnancies.
notes.C: Molar pregnancy involves abnormal trophoblastic proliferation and is not the term for embryos conceived weeks apart.
notes.E: Superfecundation involves fertilisation of separate ova from the same ovulatory cycle rather than a later pregnancy.

questions.stem: The syncytiotrophoblast differs from the cytotrophoblast in that it is

options.label: B
options.text: the stem layer for the cytotrophoblast

questions.why: Syncytiotrophoblast forms through fusion of cytotrophoblast cells into a multinucleated outer layer that does not itself divide mitotically. It invades maternal tissue during implantation and subsequently contributes to placental exchange and endocrine secretion.

notes.A: Mononuclear proliferative cells characterise cytotrophoblast, which supplies new cells to the outer syncytial layer.
notes.B: Cytotrophoblast acts as the proliferative source of syncytiotrophoblast rather than receiving new cells from it.
notes.C: The embryoblast forms embryonic lineages, whereas both trophoblastic layers arise from the outer blastocyst population.
notes.D: Heuser's membrane lines the primitive yolk sac, rather than covering the invasive outer trophoblastic layer.

questions.stem: The primary (primitive) yolk sac is lined by a thin layer called
questions.why: Heuser's membrane, also termed the exocoelomic membrane, forms from hypoblast-associated cells spreading along the internal cytotrophoblastic surface. Together with hypoblast it encloses the primitive yolk sac within the former blastocyst cavity.

notes.B: The amnion surrounds the developing amniotic cavity, rather than lining the primitive yolk sac.
notes.C: The chorion comprises trophoblast and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm, rather than the primitive yolk sac lining.
notes.D: Reichert's membrane is an extraembryonic basement membrane described particularly in rodents, not the human exocoelomic lining.
notes.E: Decidua is modified maternal endometrium surrounding the implanting conceptus rather than a yolk sac membrane.

questions.stem: Extraembryonic somatic (parietal) mesoderm is associated with the amnion and chorion, whereas extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm covers the
questions.why: Extraembryonic mesoderm separates into somatic and splanchnic layers as the chorionic cavity develops. Somatic mesoderm associates with amnion and trophoblast, whereas splanchnic mesoderm accompanies endodermal structures including the yolk sac and allantois.

notes.A: Decidua basalis is maternal endometrium at the implantation site rather than an extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm derivative.
notes.C: The amnion is associated externally with somatic extraembryonic mesoderm rather than the yolk sac-associated splanchnic layer.
notes.D: Chorion frondosum is villous chorion containing somatic extraembryonic mesoderm, not the specified endoderm-associated structures.
notes.E: The body stalk comprises extraembryonic mesoderm connecting the embryo to chorion, rather than a splanchnic covering.

questions.stem: The umbilical cord develops from the
questions.why: The connecting stalk suspends the developing embryo within the chorionic cavity and contains extraembryonic mesoderm. As the amnion expands, it encloses the stalk and associated yolk sac structures to form the developing umbilical cord.

notes.A: Amnion provides the cord's external covering, but the connecting stalk forms its principal underlying structural precursor.
notes.B: Chorion laeve forms the smooth chorionic membrane rather than the mesodermal connection forming the cord.
notes.D: The notochord establishes the embryonic axial organisation and does not form the external umbilical connection.
notes.E: The allantois contributes structures within the connecting stalk but does not alone generate the entire cord.

questions.stem: The villous chorion related to the decidua basalis, forming the fetal placenta, is the
questions.why: Chorionic villi proliferate and persist adjacent to the decidua basalis, producing the chorion frondosum. This bushy chorionic region contributes the fetal placenta, while villi facing the decidua capsularis largely regress.

notes.A: Amniochorion refers to the associated fetal membranes rather than specifically identifying the villous fetal placental region.
notes.B: Decidua parietalis is maternal endometrium away from the implantation site, not the fetal villous component.
notes.C: Heuser's membrane lines the primitive yolk sac and does not form the villous fetal placenta.
notes.E: Chorion laeve is the relatively smooth region where villi regress, rather than the persistent villous placenta.

questions.stem: The connective tissue of the umbilical cord that cushions its vessels is
questions.why: Wharton's jelly is specialised mucous connective tissue surrounding the umbilical arteries and vein. Its hydrated extracellular matrix resists compression and helps protect cord vessels from deformation during fetal movement.

notes.A: Reichert's membrane is an extraembryonic basement membrane described in certain mammals, rather than umbilical connective tissue.
notes.B: Heuser's membrane forms the primitive yolk sac lining and does not provide structural support to cord vessels.
notes.C: Nabothian cysts contain cervical mucus, rather than the specialised connective tissue surrounding fetal umbilical vessels.
notes.D: Waldeyer's ring describes pharyngeal lymphoid tissue and is unrelated to the mucous matrix of the cord.

questions.stem: Early in development the umbilical cord contains two arteries and two veins; later there remains
questions.why: Initially paired umbilical veins accompany paired arteries, but the right umbilical vein regresses during development. The definitive cord therefore usually contains two arteries carrying fetal blood placentally and one vein returning oxygenated blood.

notes.B: A single umbilical artery can occur as a congenital variant, rather than representing normal definitive cord anatomy.
notes.C: Both umbilical veins are initially present, but normally only the left persists within the mature cord.
notes.D: The normal cord retains paired arteries and one vein, rather than one artery and paired veins.
notes.E: Three arteries are not the conventional arrangement of fetal vessels within a normally developed umbilical cord.

questions.stem: A chorionic villus becomes a tertiary villus when it acquires

options.label: B
options.text: blood vessels in its mesenchymal core

questions.why: Primary villi consist of trophoblast, and secondary villi acquire a mesenchymal core. Differentiation of fetal capillaries within that core creates tertiary villi, enabling establishment of a functional fetal placental exchange circulation.

notes.A: Amniotic epithelium covers the amniotic membrane rather than defining the vascular maturation of chorionic villi.
notes.C: A mesenchymal core identifies a secondary villus before fetal capillary development establishes the tertiary stage.
notes.D: Syncytiotrophoblast already covers earlier villous stages and therefore does not distinguish the vascular tertiary villus.
notes.E: Decidua is maternal endometrium and is not the developmental layer acquired within tertiary fetal villi.

questions.stem: Villi that anchor the placenta to the decidua basalis are the
questions.why: Anchoring villi extend towards the maternal basal plate and attach through trophoblastic structures to decidual tissue. Their mechanical role contrasts with freely branching villi that provide extensive surfaces for maternal–fetal exchange.

notes.A: Stem villi provide structural support and branching origins, but attachment specifically identifies anchoring villous structures.
notes.B: The chorionic plate forms the fetal placental surface, rather than individual villi attaching to maternal tissue.
notes.D: Free terminal villi specialise in exchange within maternal intervillous blood rather than attaching to the decidua.
notes.E: Primary villi represent an early developmental stage, rather than a classification based on maternal attachment.

questions.stem: In the mature (late) placenta, the number of layers separating maternal and fetal blood is
questions.why: At thin exchange regions of the mature placenta, the barrier can be described as syncytiotrophoblast, closely apposed or fused basal laminae and fetal capillary endothelium. Earlier villi possess additional cellular and stromal components.

notes.A: Two layers omit the basal lamina component when using the conventional three-part description of the mature barrier.
notes.B: A single layer would omit distinct fetal endothelial and trophoblastic components separating the two circulations.
notes.C: Five layers more closely resemble a thicker earlier villous barrier containing additional cellular or stromal structures.
notes.E: Six layers may be counted in earlier placental descriptions, before substantial thinning of the exchange barrier.

questions.stem: Placenta accreta is characterised by

options.label: B
options.text: the placenta overlying the internal os

questions.why: In accreta the decidua basalis is deficient so villi adhere abnormally; percreta is penetration through the myometrium; praevia overlies the os.

questions.stem: At term the normal amniotic fluid volume is about
questions.why: Amniotic fluid volume generally reaches a maximum during late pregnancy and subsequently declines towards delivery. Approximately 800–1000 mL is a conventional near-term estimate, with considerable physiological variation and dependence on gestational age.

notes.B: One hundred to two hundred millilitres is substantially below conventional near-term amniotic fluid volume estimates.
notes.C: Two to three litres exceeds ordinary near-term volume and may represent excessive amniotic fluid accumulation.
notes.D: Fifty to one hundred millilitres is far below the expected volume surrounding a normally developed term fetus.
notes.E: One and a half to two litres is above the conventional near-term central estimate for fluid volume.

questions.stem: From about 20 weeks to term, the main source of amniotic fluid is
questions.why: After fetal skin becomes keratinised, fetal urine supplies most amniotic fluid, with pulmonary fluid also contributing. Fetal swallowing and intramembranous absorption remove fluid, maintaining a dynamic balance throughout later pregnancy.

notes.A: Amniotic epithelium participates in fluid transport but is not the major late-gestation source compared with fetal urine.
notes.C: Maternal fluid contributes indirectly to fetal and placental water balance rather than directly supplying most late amniotic fluid.
notes.D: Fetal lungs contribute liquid to the amniotic cavity, but urine generally provides a greater volume.
notes.E: Transcutaneous exchange is more important earlier in development, before fetal skin keratinisation limits this pathway.

questions.stem: After delivery, the placenta normally separates through the
questions.why: After birth, uterine contraction reduces the placental attachment area and produces shearing at the maternal interface. Normal separation occurs predominantly within the spongy layer of the decidua basalis, allowing placental expulsion.

notes.A: The myometrium contracts to assist separation, but normal placental detachment occurs within the decidual attachment layer.
notes.B: Decidua parietalis lines regions away from the implantation site rather than forming the main separation plane.
notes.D: Chorion laeve forms smooth fetal membranes and is not the principal maternal placental separation interface.
notes.E: Amnion covers fetal surfaces and does not provide the normal plane between placenta and uterine wall.

questions.stem: The placental hormone with growth-hormone-like actions that promotes maternal lipolysis and glucose sparing is
questions.why: Human chorionic somatomammotrophin, also called human placental lactogen, is produced by syncytiotrophoblast. Its metabolic actions contribute to maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis, helping maintain glucose availability for fetal transfer during pregnancy.

notes.A: Relaxin contributes to reproductive tissue remodelling but is not the principal growth-hormone-like placental metabolic hormone.
notes.B: Progesterone maintains pregnancy-associated uterine and endometrial functions rather than being the specified somatomammotrophic protein hormone.
notes.C: Oxytocin promotes uterine contractions and milk ejection rather than the characteristic maternal glucose-sparing metabolic adaptation.
notes.E: Human chorionic gonadotropin maintains early luteal steroidogenesis through LH receptors, rather than providing the specified lactogenic activity.

questions.stem: Gastrulation begins with the appearance of the primitive streak on the
questions.why: The primitive streak appears along the caudal midline of the epiblast during the third week. It provides the site through which epiblast cells ingress to establish definitive endoderm and intraembryonic mesoderm.

notes.A: Hypoblast contributes extraembryonic endodermal structures and does not form the primitive streak on its cranial surface.
notes.B: Trophoblast forms extraembryonic placental structures rather than the embryonic epiblast site of primitive streak formation.
notes.C: Amnion encloses the amniotic cavity but does not provide the principal epithelial substrate for gastrulation.
notes.D: The notochordal plate develops following axial cell migration, rather than preceding formation of the primitive streak.

questions.stem: Epiblast cells ingress through the primitive streak by a process called
questions.why: Epiblast cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition during gastrulation, losing epithelial polarity and reducing intercellular adhesion. These changes permit individual cells to ingress through the primitive streak and migrate into new embryonic layers.

notes.B: Cleavage involves mitotic division without substantial overall growth, rather than the epithelial changes enabling gastrulation-associated ingression.
notes.C: Apoptosis eliminates cells through programmed death, whereas ingression requires surviving cells to change adhesion and migrate.
notes.D: Compaction increases adhesion between early blastomeres, rather than reducing epithelial adhesion to facilitate primitive streak migration.
notes.E: Decidualisation modifies maternal endometrial stromal cells and does not describe the migration of embryonic epiblast cells.

questions.stem: The master inducer (a TGF-beta family member) that initiates primitive-streak formation is
questions.why: NODAL is a transforming growth factor beta-family signal important in primitive streak formation and mesendoderm specification. Its interactions with WNT, BMP and FGF signalling coordinate gastrulation, rather than acting as an isolated inducer.

notes.A: BMP4 contributes to posterior patterning and signalling interactions, but NODAL is the specified central mesendoderm-inducing signal.
notes.C: Sonic hedgehog contributes prominently to later axial patterning, rather than serving as the specified primitive streak inducer.
notes.D: CDX2 is a transcription factor associated with trophectoderm and posterior identity, not the specified extracellular signal.
notes.E: NANOG regulates pluripotency-associated transcriptional programmes rather than acting as a secreted TGF-beta-family gastrulation signal.

questions.stem: The first wave of cells migrating through the primitive streak displaces the hypoblast to become
questions.why: During gastrulation, early ingressing epiblast cells intercalate into and replace hypoblast within the embryonic disc, establishing definitive endoderm. Subsequent ingressing cells form mesoderm, while remaining epiblast contributes ectoderm.

notes.A: Notochord develops from specialised axial mesodermal cells migrating through the primitive node rather than the entire first wave.
notes.B: Neural crest arises later from the developing neural plate border, rather than directly replacing hypoblast during gastrulation.
notes.D: Intraembryonic mesoderm develops between ectoderm and endoderm following ingression, rather than forming the initial definitive epithelial replacement.
notes.E: Ectoderm derives mainly from epiblast remaining at the surface, not from cells that replace the hypoblast.

questions.stem: The notochord secretes which signalling molecule to pattern the neural tube and somites?
questions.why: Sonic hedgehog released from the notochord and subsequently the neural floor plate patterns ventral neural tube identities. Notochord-derived signals also promote sclerotome differentiation in adjacent somites, contributing to axial skeletal development.

notes.A: Human chorionic gonadotropin is principally a placental endocrine hormone rather than a notochord-derived axial patterning signal.
notes.B: WNT signals participate in neural and somitic patterning, but Sonic hedgehog provides the characteristic ventral notochordal signal.
notes.C: E-cadherin is a cell adhesion protein rather than a secreted morphogen establishing ventral neural tube identities.
notes.E: NODAL participates in gastrulation and left–right patterning rather than providing the characteristic notochordal ventralising signal.

questions.stem: The two points where ectoderm and endoderm stay fused with no intervening mesoderm are the
questions.why: At the oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes, embryonic ectoderm and endoderm remain directly apposed without intervening mesoderm. These cranial and caudal landmarks subsequently contribute to formation of the oral and terminal hindgut openings.

notes.A: Amnion and chorion are extraembryonic membranes, rather than the two bilaminar regions of the embryonic disc.
notes.B: The primitive node and streak are sites of gastrulation and mesoderm migration rather than persistent mesoderm-free membranes.
notes.C: The notochord is axial mesoderm, so its inclusion contradicts the absence of intervening mesoderm in these membranes.
notes.D: Primary and secondary yolk sacs are successive extraembryonic structures, not the cranial and caudal bilaminar membranes.

questions.stem: The human embryo has a total of how many pairs of somites?
questions.why: Approximately 42–44 pairs of somites form from paraxial mesoderm during early development. They include occipital, cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal groups, with some terminal somites subsequently regressing.

notes.B: Seven is close to the number of cervical vertebrae, not the total number of embryonic somites.
notes.C: Twelve corresponds to the usual thoracic somite group rather than the complete craniocaudal somite population.
notes.D: Twenty to twenty-five somite pairs occur during an intermediate developmental stage before the full series forms.
notes.E: Sixty exceeds the conventional total of human somite pairs formed during the early embryonic period.

questions.stem: The lateral plate mesoderm is split into somatic and splanchnic layers by the
questions.why: Spaces appearing within lateral plate mesoderm merge to form the intraembryonic coelom, separating somatic and splanchnic mesodermal layers. These layers contribute respectively to body-wall and visceral structures surrounding developing serous cavities.

notes.A: The chorionic cavity is extraembryonic and does not itself divide the intraembryonic lateral plate mesoderm.
notes.C: The neural canal forms within the neural tube and is unrelated to lateral plate mesodermal separation.
notes.D: The primitive groove provides a site for gastrulation rather than forming the future intraembryonic body cavities.
notes.E: The amniotic cavity surrounds the embryo dorsally and does not split lateral plate mesoderm into its layers.

questions.stem: The embryonic period of organogenesis, when the embryo is most sensitive to teratogens, spans weeks
questions.why: Weeks three through eight after fertilisation encompass the major embryonic period of organogenesis. Disruption during this interval can produce major structural malformations because organ primordia are undergoing differentiation and morphogenesis.

notes.A: Weeks eight through twelve span the transition towards the fetal period, when growth and functional maturation predominate.
notes.B: Weeks twelve through sixteen belong to fetal development, although selected organs remain vulnerable to harmful exposures.
notes.D: The first two weeks principally involve cleavage and implantation, before the major period of organ formation.
notes.E: Weeks nine through twelve are early fetal weeks rather than the principal embryonic organogenesis interval.

questions.stem: Insufficient migration of mesoderm around the oropharyngeal membrane is associated with
questions.why: Deficient cranial mesoderm underlies holoprosencephaly (failure of forebrain cleavage); deficient caudal mesoderm gives sirenomelia.

questions.stem: Caudal dysgenesis with fused lower limbs (the 'mermaid' malformation) from insufficient caudal mesoderm is
questions.why: Sirenomelia is a severe caudal developmental anomaly featuring fusion of the lower limbs and frequent genitourinary abnormalities. Defective caudal mesoderm development and abnormal vascular supply are proposed mechanisms, rather than a single universally established cause.

notes.A: Holoprosencephaly involves abnormal forebrain division rather than the characteristic fused lower limbs of severe caudal maldevelopment.
notes.B: Omphalocele involves herniation of abdominal contents into a membrane-covered umbilical sac rather than limb fusion.
notes.C: Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect with exposed herniated viscera, not the characteristic caudal limb anomaly.
notes.D: Meromelia denotes partial absence of a limb, rather than the characteristic fusion of the lower limbs.

questions.stem: Remnants of the primitive streak that persist can give rise, in the newborn, to a
questions.why: Persistent pluripotent cells associated with the primitive streak can give rise to sacrococcygeal teratomas. These tumours may contain differentiated tissues from multiple germ layers, reflecting their developmental cellular origin near the caudal embryo.

notes.B: Wilms tumour arises from abnormal renal precursor development rather than residual pluripotent primitive streak cells.
notes.C: Neuroblastoma originates from sympathetic neural crest-derived precursors rather than the characteristic caudal primitive streak remnants.
notes.D: Hydatidiform mole involves abnormal conceptus genetics and trophoblast proliferation, rather than residual primitive streak tissue.
notes.E: Ovarian dermoid cysts are germ-cell tumours, but the specified caudal embryonic remnants produce sacrococcygeal teratomas.

questions.stem: New blood vessels forming de novo from angioblasts that differentiate from mesenchyme is called
questions.why: Vasculogenesis creates new vascular structures through differentiation and assembly of mesoderm-derived angioblasts into endothelial networks. Angiogenesis subsequently expands or remodels vascular beds through growth from existing vessels.

notes.B: Angiogenesis generates new vessels from pre-existing vascular structures, rather than establishing endothelial networks directly from precursors.
notes.C: Haematopoiesis produces blood cellular elements rather than specifically assembling endothelial cells into new vascular channels.
notes.D: Angioplasty is a clinical intervention to enlarge narrowed vessels, not a process of embryonic vascular development.
notes.E: Arteriogenesis involves enlargement and remodelling of arterial pathways, rather than initial endothelial network formation from angioblasts.

questions.stem: The primordium of the heart first forms in the
questions.why: Cardiac progenitors arise within splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm in the cranial cardiogenic region. Their organisation into heart fields precedes formation and folding of the primitive heart tube during early embryogenesis.

notes.A: Neural crest contributes to outflow tract and other cardiovascular structures, but does not form the initial cardiac field.
notes.C: The sinus venosus develops as a venous inflow component after establishment of the early cardiac primordium.
notes.D: The bulbus cordis is a region of the developing heart tube, rather than its initial cardiogenic mesodermal source.
notes.E: Septum transversum contributes to diaphragm development and related tissues, rather than constituting the initial heart primordium.

questions.stem: The single primitive heart tube forms by
questions.why: Lateral embryonic folding brings the paired endocardial tubes towards the ventral midline, where they fuse to form the primitive heart tube. Surrounding cardiogenic mesoderm contributes myocardial tissue and associated cardiac layers.

notes.A: The primitive heart tube develops from cardiogenic mesoderm rather than budding from an already formed aorta.
notes.B: Outflow tract division occurs later during cardiac septation, rather than producing the initial single heart tube.
notes.D: The bulbus cordis is a region of the established primitive heart tube and does not initiate its formation.
notes.E: The sinus venosus develops at the venous end of the heart tube rather than generating it through folding.

questions.stem: The cephalic (arterial) end of the bulbus cordis elongates to become the
questions.why: The arterial end of the developing heart tube includes the truncus arteriosus, continuous proximally with the conus cordis. Subsequent outflow tract remodelling and septation produce the proximal great arterial pathways.

notes.A: The primitive atrium develops near the venous inflow region rather than the cephalic arterial end.
notes.B: The conus cordis is the more proximal outflow component, rather than the distal truncal arterial segment.
notes.C: The aortic sac lies beyond the truncus arteriosus and supplies developing pharyngeal arch arteries.
notes.E: The sinus venosus receives embryonic systemic veins at the opposite, venous end of the cardiac tube.

questions.stem: To accommodate elongation, the heart tube bends from left to right forming the
questions.why: Rapid cardiac tube elongation within the pericardial cavity produces looping, normally with rightward bending of the ventricular region. This bulboventricular loop establishes spatial relationships necessary for subsequent chamber formation and septation.

notes.A: Sinus venarum denotes the smooth adult right atrial wall formed by incorporation of systemic venous tissue.
notes.B: Septum spurium is associated with embryonic venous valve development rather than elongation and looping of ventricles.
notes.C: Crista terminalis separates smooth and trabeculated right atrial regions rather than describing the early cardiac loop.
notes.D: Septum intermedium arises from fused atrioventricular endocardial cushions, not the bending of the elongated heart tube.

questions.stem: The superior and inferior endocardial cushions fuse to partition the atrioventricular canal, forming the
questions.why: Superior and inferior atrioventricular endocardial cushions grow and fuse to form the septum intermedium. This partitions the initially common atrioventricular canal into right and left openings and contributes to subsequent septation.

notes.B: Septum primum grows from the atrial roof towards the cushions, rather than forming directly from their fusion.
notes.C: Septum secundum develops as an atrial septal fold rather than the partition produced by atrioventricular cushion fusion.
notes.D: Septum spurium arises in association with sinus venosus valve folds rather than the common atrioventricular canal.
notes.E: The aorticopulmonary septum partitions the arterial outflow tract, not the common atrioventricular opening between chambers.

questions.stem: The gap between the growing edge of the septum primum and the endocardial cushions is the
questions.why: Ostium primum is the transient opening beneath the advancing septum primum and above the atrioventricular endocardial cushions. It permits atrial communication until the septum reaches and fuses with the cushions.

notes.A: The coronary sinus drains cardiac venous blood and does not represent a transient opening beneath septum primum.
notes.C: Ostium secundum develops through perforation of the upper septum primum as ostium primum approaches closure.
notes.D: Foramen ovale is associated with the later septum secundum and flap-valve arrangement rather than this initial gap.
notes.E: The sinoatrial orifice connects sinus venosus and primitive atrium, rather than the two developing atrial compartments.

questions.stem: Before the ostium primum closes, perforations in the septum primum form the
questions.why: Programmed cell loss and remodelling produce perforations in the superior septum primum that merge as ostium secundum. This preserves fetal interatrial communication when the inferior ostium primum closes against the cushions.

notes.A: Sinus venarum is the smooth venous portion of the right atrium, not a perforation within septum primum.
notes.B: Septum spurium forms near the embryonic venous valves, rather than from perforations in the primary atrial septum.
notes.D: Foramen ovale is the later opening associated with septum secundum, overlapping the ostium secundum region.
notes.E: Ostium primum is the original inferior opening beneath septum primum, rather than its later superior perforation.

questions.stem: The septum secundum differs from the septum primum in that it is

options.label: C
options.text: the floor of the coronary sinus

questions.why: Septum secundum forms a thicker muscular fold to the right of septum primum and incompletely overlaps ostium secundum. Its inferior opening forms the foramen ovale, with the thinner septum primum acting as a flap.

notes.A: Endocardial cushions contribute to closure of the inferior atrial opening, rather than generating the entire septum secundum.
notes.B: Sinus venosus contributes to venous atrial structures, whereas septum secundum develops within the atrial septal region.
notes.C: The coronary sinus develops from left sinus horn derivatives, not from the thicker secondary atrial septum.
notes.E: The thin mobile flap is septum primum, whereas septum secundum provides the relatively firm overlapping rim.

questions.stem: In the fetus the septum primum acts at the foramen ovale as a

options.label: E
options.text: flap valve allowing only right-to-left flow

questions.why: Septum primum forms a flexible flap on the left side of the foramen ovale. Higher fetal right atrial pressure usually permits right-to-left passage, while reversed pressure presses the flap against its rim.

notes.A: A rigid fixed partition would prevent the pressure-dependent flap movement required for fetal interatrial blood flow.
notes.B: The usual fetal pressure gradient favours right-to-left flow, rather than the reversed direction stated in this option.
notes.C: The septum primum functions through passive flap displacement rather than active contraction of a muscular sphincter.
notes.D: Coronary sinus derives mainly from the left sinus horn, not from the mobile primary atrial septum.

questions.stem: The crista terminalis of the adult right atrium is the persistent
questions.why: Fused venous valves form the septum spurium, persisting as the crista terminalis between smooth and rough right atrium.

questions.stem: Absorption of the right horn of the sinus venosus forms the
questions.why: The right horn of the sinus venosus becomes incorporated into the right atrial wall, creating the smooth-walled sinus venarum. This contrasts with the trabeculated primitive atrial portion containing pectinate muscles.

notes.A: Pulmonary venous incorporation contributes to the smooth left atrial wall rather than the right sinus horn derivative.
notes.C: The left atrium forms from primitive atrial and pulmonary venous components rather than right sinus horn incorporation.
notes.D: Coronary sinus develops principally from the left horn of the sinus venosus, not its enlarged right horn.
notes.E: The right auricle retains trabeculated primitive atrial tissue rather than the incorporated smooth systemic venous component.

questions.stem: The coronary sinus develops from the

options.label: C
options.text: left horn of the sinus venosus

options.label: D
options.text: right horn of the sinus venosus

questions.why: The left horn of the sinus venosus becomes reduced as systemic venous return shifts rightward, persisting principally as the coronary sinus. Associated left-sided venous remnants also contribute to the oblique vein of the left atrium.

notes.A: Septum primum contributes to atrial septation and the foramen ovale flap rather than coronary venous drainage.
notes.B: Left common cardinal venous tissue contributes associated structures, but the coronary sinus principally represents the left sinus horn.
notes.D: The right sinus horn is incorporated into the smooth right atrial wall rather than becoming the coronary sinus.
notes.E: Pulmonary veins contribute to left atrial development and do not form the major coronary venous collecting channel.

questions.stem: The smooth part of the left atrium is formed by absorption of the

options.label: E
options.text: right horn of the sinus venosus

questions.why: Incorporation of the common pulmonary vein and its branches into the developing left atrium creates much of its smooth posterior wall. The trabeculated left auricle retains tissue derived from the primitive atrium.

notes.A: The coronary sinus drains cardiac veins into the right atrium rather than forming the smooth left atrial wall.
notes.B: Left venous valve remnants participate in atrial septal development, not incorporation of pulmonary venous drainage.
notes.C: Truncus arteriosus contributes to great arterial outflow structures rather than the pulmonary venous portion of the atrium.
notes.E: The right sinus horn forms the smooth systemic venous region of the right atrium, not left atrium.

questions.stem: The lower edge of the septum secundum seen in the right atrium becomes the
questions.why: The muscular rim surrounding the adult fossa ovalis is conventionally termed the limbus or annulus ovalis. It corresponds largely to the secondary septal fold, whereas the fossa floor derives from septum primum.

notes.A: Crista terminalis marks the boundary between smooth and trabeculated portions of the right atrium, not the fossa rim.
notes.B: The coronary sinus valve derives from the right venous valve, rather than the rim of septum secundum.
notes.C: Septum spurium is an embryonic structure associated with venous valves, not the mature fossa ovalis rim.
notes.D: Sinus venarum denotes the smooth right atrial region incorporated from systemic venous tissue rather than the septal rim.

questions.stem: A secundum-type atrial septal defect may arise from excessive resorption of the septum primum or

options.label: B
options.text: failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse

questions.why: An ostium secundum atrial septal defect may result from excessive loss of septum primum tissue or insufficient development of the secondary septal fold. Either mechanism leaves inadequate overlap to close the interatrial communication.

notes.B: Endocardial cushion fusion failure is associated with ostium primum defects and atrioventricular septal abnormalities rather than typical secundum defects.
notes.C: Deficient conal swellings affect ventricular outflow tract separation rather than the overlap of developing atrial septa.
notes.D: Normal spiral outflow tract septation separates the great arteries and does not directly produce a secundum atrial defect.
notes.E: Sinus venosus abnormalities may cause distinct atrial septal defects, rather than the classic mechanism of ostium secundum defects.

questions.stem: The muscular part of the definitive interventricular septum develops from the
questions.why: The primary muscular interventricular septum grows between the expanding ventricular chambers. It forms most of the definitive ventricular partition, while the remaining superior communication is closed through contributions from cushion and outflow tissues.

notes.A: The aorticopulmonary septum separates developing arterial outflow channels rather than forming most of the muscular ventricular septum.
notes.C: Endocardial cushions contribute to the membranous septal region, rather than supplying the bulk of muscular septal tissue.
notes.D: Bulbar ridges participate in outflow tract partitioning and membranous septal closure, rather than the primary muscular septum.
notes.E: Septum secundum participates in atrial separation and does not form the muscular partition between the ventricles.

questions.stem: The membranous part of the interventricular septum is formed by the endocardial cushions and the
questions.why: The membranous interventricular septum forms where atrioventricular cushion tissue and conal septal structures unite with the muscular septum. Failure of this coordinated closure can leave a perimembranous ventricular septal defect.

notes.A: Crista terminalis is a right atrial landmark rather than a component of the membranous ventricular septum.
notes.B: Venous valves form or contribute to atrial inflow structures, rather than closing the superior interventricular communication.
notes.D: The primary muscular septum provides the attachment boundary but does not itself supply the specified conal tissue contribution.
notes.E: Septum primum participates in atrial septation, rather than forming the membranous ventricular partition.

questions.stem: Partitioning of the outflow tract (truncus arteriosus and conus cordis) into aorta and pulmonary trunk is achieved by a spiral septum derived from
questions.why: Cardiac neural crest cells migrate into the developing outflow tract and contribute importantly to its septation, alongside mesodermal populations. Coordinated remodelling separates the aortic and pulmonary channels and aligns them with the ventricles.

notes.A: Endoderm provides inductive signals during development but is not the principal migratory population specified for outflow septation.
notes.B: Sinus venosus contributes to cardiac venous inflow structures rather than the neural crest-associated arterial outflow partition.
notes.C: Septum primum divides the developing atria and does not supply the cell population responsible for arterial septation.
notes.E: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, while cardiac neural crest is especially important for the specified outflow tract septation.

questions.stem: Failure of the truncoconal swellings to grow at all, leaving a single outflow vessel over a VSD, is
questions.why: Persistent truncus arteriosus, also called common arterial trunk, results from failure to separate the embryonic outflow tract adequately. One arterial vessel supplies systemic, pulmonary and coronary circulations, typically overriding a ventricular septal defect.

notes.A: Transposition involves separate great arteries with abnormal ventricular connections, rather than persistence of one common arterial trunk.
notes.B: Tetralogy of Fallot involves outflow septal malalignment and obstruction, but usually retains separate aortic and pulmonary outlets.
notes.C: Coarctation describes narrowing of the aorta rather than failure of the common embryonic arterial outlet to divide.
notes.D: Dextrocardia describes rightward cardiac orientation and does not itself establish persistence of an undivided arterial trunk.

questions.stem: Transposition of the great arteries results from the truncoconal swellings failing to
questions.why: In the classical embryological model, abnormal spiralling and alignment of the outflow tract lead to transposition of the great arteries. The aorta connects to the right ventricle and pulmonary artery to the left.

notes.B: Endocardial cushion abnormalities can disrupt atrioventricular septation, rather than defining the reversed great arterial connections of transposition.
notes.C: Sinus venosus incorporation forms parts of the atrial inflow structures rather than determining normal great arterial alignment.
notes.D: Septum primum contributes to atrial partitioning and its fusion is not the specific outflow alignment mechanism.
notes.E: Division of the common atrioventricular canal establishes separate inflow openings rather than the ventricular connections of great arteries.

questions.stem: Tetralogy of Fallot arises from a single error in which the conus septum develops
questions.why: Anterosuperior deviation of the outlet septum is the classical anatomical basis of tetralogy of Fallot. It produces right ventricular outflow obstruction, a malalignment ventricular septal defect and overriding aorta, with secondary right ventricular hypertrophy.

notes.A: Sinus venosus forms venous inflow structures and does not explain displacement of the ventricular outlet septum.
notes.C: Posterior deviation does not describe the characteristic anterosuperior outlet septal displacement associated with tetralogy of Fallot.
notes.D: Neural crest abnormalities can contribute to outflow defects, but total absence is not the specific anatomical malalignment described.
notes.E: The defect involves abnormal outlet septal position rather than a normal septum developing two separate spiral turns.

questions.stem: A heart that loops to the right as a mirror image, with its apex pointing right, is
questions.why: Dextrocardia (reversed looping) points the apex to the right, often with situs inversus of all organs.

questions.stem: A heart lying partly or wholly outside the thorax, from failure of the sternum to develop, is
questions.why: Ectopia cordis describes partial or complete displacement of the heart outside the thoracic cavity, usually through a ventral body-wall defect. Abnormal development or fusion of sternal and adjacent structures can contribute.

notes.A: A common ventricle is an internal chamber malformation rather than external displacement of the developing heart.
notes.B: Persistent truncus arteriosus involves an undivided arterial outlet, not a defect exposing the heart outside the thorax.
notes.C: Tetralogy of Fallot combines characteristic intracardiac and outflow abnormalities rather than external cardiac displacement.
notes.E: Dextrocardia describes rightward cardiac orientation and can occur with the heart remaining entirely within the thorax.

questions.stem: In the fetus, the vessel carrying the most oxygen-rich blood (about 80% saturation) is the
questions.why: Placental oxygen exchange supplies fetal blood returning through the umbilical vein, which has the highest oxygen saturation among major fetal vessels. Subsequent mixing with systemic venous blood progressively lowers saturation.

notes.A: Umbilical arteries convey relatively oxygen-poor fetal blood towards the placenta for gas and nutrient exchange.
notes.B: The descending aorta receives mixed ventricular output, including blood entering through the ductus arteriosus, with lower saturation.
notes.C: Inferior caval blood includes oxygenated placental return mixed with lower-body systemic venous blood, reducing its saturation.
notes.D: The pulmonary trunk receives right ventricular output containing considerable systemic venous blood rather than the richest placental return.

questions.stem: The ductus venosus shunts oxygen-rich umbilical-vein blood directly into the
questions.why: The ductus venosus channels a portion of oxygen-rich umbilical venous blood from the hepatic portal region towards the inferior vena cava. This bypasses hepatic sinusoids and facilitates rapid delivery to the heart.

notes.B: The ductus venosus originates near the portal region, but its downstream drainage is towards the inferior vena cava.
notes.C: Blood reaches the right atrium through the inferior vena cava rather than directly from the ductus venosus.
notes.D: Pulmonary trunk receives ventricular output downstream of the heart, rather than the hepatic venous bypass itself.
notes.E: The coronary sinus drains myocardial veins into the right atrium and does not receive the ductus venosus.

questions.stem: Oxygen-rich IVC blood is preferentially streamed across the foramen ovale to the left atrium by the
questions.why: Preferential fetal streaming directs relatively oxygen-rich inferior caval blood towards the foramen ovale. The inferior caval valve and atrial septal geometry, including the crista dividens, help separate this stream from superior caval return.

notes.A: Superior caval blood preferentially enters the right ventricular pathway rather than providing the specified oxygen-rich inferior caval stream.
notes.C: Crista terminalis separates smooth and trabeculated right atrial regions and is not the main streaming structure described.
notes.D: Septum spurium is associated with embryonic venous valves but is not the specified principal fetal streaming apparatus.
notes.E: Coronary sinus carries myocardial venous blood rather than directing oxygen-rich placental blood across the foramen ovale.

questions.stem: In utero the ductus arteriosus carries approximately what proportion of right-ventricular output to the descending aorta?
questions.why: About 80-90% of RV output bypasses the high-resistance lungs via the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta.

questions.stem: The nerve that loops posteriorly around the ductus arteriosus/ligamentum arteriosum is the
questions.why: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve passes beneath the aortic arch near the ductus arteriosus and its later ligamentous remnant. Its recurrent course reflects descent of the heart and remodelling of embryonic arch arteries.

notes.A: The vagus gives rise to the recurrent branch, but its main trunk does not form the specified loop.
notes.B: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the right subclavian artery rather than the left ductal region.
notes.C: The sympathetic chain lies paravertebrally and does not form the recurrent loop around the ligamentum arteriosum.
notes.E: The phrenic nerve descends anterior to the lung root towards the diaphragm rather than looping beneath the arch.

questions.stem: After birth the ductus arteriosus normally closes within
questions.why: In healthy term newborns, rising oxygen tension and reduced prostaglandin-mediated dilation usually produce functional ductus arteriosus closure within the first day or two. Anatomical obliteration takes considerably longer and varies with maturity.

notes.A: One to two weeks better approximates later remodelling in some descriptions than the typical initial functional closure interval.
notes.B: Ductal constriction begins after birth but complete functional closure does not routinely occur within just a few minutes.
notes.C: Three months is much later than the usual functional closure of the ductus in healthy term newborns.
notes.D: One hour may be sufficient for substantial constriction, but is too early as a general functional closure estimate.

questions.stem: Closure of the ductus venosus after birth is promoted by

options.label: A
options.text: a fall in prostaglandins after cord clamping

options.label: C
options.text: the first breath inflating the lungs

questions.why: Cord clamping and a decrease in prostaglandins close the ductus venosus, which becomes the ligamentum venosum.

questions.stem: At birth the foramen ovale closes because
questions.why: Lung aeration reduces pulmonary vascular resistance and increases pulmonary venous return to the left atrium. Interruption of placental venous return reduces right atrial filling, allowing higher left atrial pressure to close the foramen ovale flap.

notes.A: The umbilical vein ceases carrying placental blood after cord interruption rather than dilating to close the interatrial flap.
notes.C: Higher right atrial pressure would favour opening the fetal flap rather than pressing it closed from the left.
notes.D: Ductal patency affects arterial shunting but does not directly generate the atrial pressure gradient that closes the flap.
notes.E: Pulmonary resistance normally falls with lung aeration, increasing left atrial filling rather than sustaining fetal shunting.

questions.stem: After birth, the ductus venosus becomes the
questions.why: Following interruption of umbilical venous flow, the ductus venosus closes and undergoes fibrous obliteration. Its adult remnant is the ligamentum venosum in the liver, marking the former hepatic bypass.

notes.A: Medial umbilical ligaments derive from obliterated distal umbilical arteries rather than the fetal hepatic venous channel.
notes.B: Fossa ovalis represents the former interatrial foramen ovale, not the remnant of the ductus venosus.
notes.D: Ligamentum teres hepatis derives from the left umbilical vein, which previously supplied the ductus venosus region.
notes.E: Ligamentum arteriosum derives from the ductus arteriosus connecting pulmonary and systemic arterial circulations before birth.

questions.stem: The pharyngeal arches first appear on the embryo during the
questions.why: Pharyngeal arches become externally evident during the fourth embryonic week as paired mesenchymal swellings in the head and neck. Their coordinated development contributes to craniofacial skeletal, muscular, vascular and neural structures.

notes.B: The second week principally establishes the bilaminar embryonic disc before pharyngeal arch morphogenesis becomes apparent.
notes.C: By the eighth week substantial differentiation of pharyngeal arch derivatives has occurred rather than their first appearance.
notes.D: The twelfth week is within the fetal period, well after the arches initially develop in the embryo.
notes.E: During the sixth week the arches are already undergoing remodelling, rather than appearing for the first time.

questions.stem: The mesenchyme forming the core of each pharyngeal arch is derived mainly from
questions.why: Pharyngeal arch mesenchyme contains substantial neural crest-derived populations alongside mesodermal cells. Neural crest contributes prominently to skeletal and connective tissues, while mesoderm supplies much of the arch musculature and vascular endothelium.

notes.A: Endoderm lines internal pharyngeal pouches and provides signals rather than forming most of the arch mesenchymal core.
notes.C: Paraxial mesoderm contributes to muscular populations, but neural crest also supplies extensive arch skeletal and connective tissue.
notes.D: Lateral plate mesoderm contributes selected arch components rather than being the principal source of all arch mesenchyme.
notes.E: Surface ectoderm covers arches externally, rather than forming their predominant internal mesenchymal cell population.

questions.stem: The external grooves between the pharyngeal arches, lined by ectoderm, are the pharyngeal
questions.why: Pharyngeal clefts or grooves are ectoderm-lined external depressions between adjacent arches. The first cleft contributes to the external acoustic meatus, while the more caudal clefts are normally covered and largely disappear.

notes.A: Arches are mesenchymal swellings themselves rather than the external ectodermal grooves separating successive swellings.
notes.B: Placodes are specialised ectodermal thickenings contributing sensory structures, rather than the grooves between pharyngeal arches.
notes.D: Pouches are endoderm-lined internal outgrowths from the primitive pharynx, opposite the external pharyngeal clefts.
notes.E: Membranes occur where cleft ectoderm and pouch endoderm approach one another, rather than describing external grooves alone.

questions.stem: The internal outpocketings between the arches, lined by endoderm, are the pharyngeal
questions.why: Pharyngeal pouches are endoderm-lined outgrowths of the primitive pharynx between adjacent arch regions. Their epithelial derivatives contribute to structures including the middle ear cavity, tonsillar epithelium, thymus and parathyroid glands.

notes.A: Grooves are external ectoderm-lined depressions rather than the internal endodermal outpocketings of the embryonic pharynx.
notes.B: Pharyngeal membranes develop where pouch endoderm and cleft ectoderm approach, rather than constituting the internal outgrowths themselves.
notes.C: The cervical sinus arises from overgrowth of external clefts rather than being the collective name for internal endodermal pouches.
notes.E: Clefts are external ectoderm-lined spaces, while pouches project internally from the endodermal pharyngeal lining.

questions.stem: Which pharyngeal arch is transient and accounts for the irregular numbering 1,2,3,4,6?
questions.why: The traditional numbering of human pharyngeal arches skips the fifth because it is absent or very rudimentary and transient in standard descriptions. The recognisable functional arch groups are numbered one, two, three, four and six.

notes.A: The first arch produces major mandibular and maxillary derivatives and is not the skipped rudimentary arch.
notes.B: The second arch forms characteristic hyoid and facial musculature derivatives, rather than disappearing without identifiable contributions.
notes.C: The sixth arch contributes important laryngeal and arterial derivatives and therefore remains represented in standard numbering.
notes.D: The third arch contributes stylopharyngeus and skeletal derivatives, rather than accounting for the irregular arch numbering.

questions.stem: Each pharyngeal arch is a self-contained module containing a cartilage bar, a muscle group, an artery and
questions.why: Each pharyngeal arch contains a characteristic skeletal or cartilaginous component, muscle precursor population, arterial channel and cranial nerve association. These relationships help trace adult structures even when derivatives migrate during development.

notes.B: Somites are segmented paraxial mesodermal structures and are not the characteristic nerve component of individual arches.
notes.C: Lymphatic vessels develop within many tissues but do not replace the characteristic cranial nerve associated with each arch.
notes.D: Placodes contribute selected sensory structures but are not the specified innervation component of a pharyngeal arch.
notes.E: Dermatomes represent segmental cutaneous sensory territories rather than the characteristic cranial nerve association of pharyngeal arch derivatives.

questions.stem: The nerve of the first pharyngeal arch is the
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve is associated with the first pharyngeal arch, with its mandibular division supplying the arch-derived muscles of mastication. Maxillary and mandibular sensory branches serve territories related to first arch prominences.

notes.A: The hypoglossal nerve supplies most tongue muscles derived from occipital somites rather than first arch musculature.
notes.C: The facial nerve supplies second arch-derived facial expression muscles, rather than the first arch muscles of mastication.
notes.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the third arch-derived stylopharyngeus muscle rather than first arch muscular derivatives.
notes.E: The vagus supplies fourth and sixth arch-related musculature through pharyngeal and laryngeal branches rather than first arch muscles.

questions.stem: The nerve of the second pharyngeal arch is the
questions.why: The facial nerve is the characteristic nerve of the second pharyngeal arch. It supplies derivatives including muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric despite their varied adult locations.

notes.A: The vagus supplies musculature associated primarily with fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches rather than second arch derivatives.
notes.B: The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, rather than the characteristic second arch facial muscle population.
notes.D: The trigeminal mandibular division supplies first arch muscles, notably muscles of mastication, rather than second arch musculature.
notes.E: The glossopharyngeal nerve is associated with the third arch and innervates stylopharyngeus rather than facial expression muscles.

questions.stem: The nerve of the third pharyngeal arch is the
questions.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve is associated with the third pharyngeal arch and provides motor innervation to stylopharyngeus. Its relationship to posterior tongue and pharyngeal territories reflects the development of this arch region.

notes.A: The trigeminal nerve is associated primarily with first arch derivatives rather than the third arch stylopharyngeus.
notes.B: The vagus supplies fourth and sixth arch-associated musculature, rather than the characteristic third arch motor derivative.
notes.C: Hypoglossal fibres supply most tongue muscles derived from occipital somites, not third arch stylopharyngeus.
notes.E: The facial nerve is associated with second arch musculature rather than the third pharyngeal arch.

questions.stem: The fourth pharyngeal arch is supplied by which branch of the vagus nerve?
questions.why: The superior laryngeal branch of the vagus is conventionally associated with fourth arch derivatives, particularly cricothyroid through its external branch. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles associated with the sixth arch.

notes.A: Recurrent laryngeal innervation is associated chiefly with sixth arch-derived intrinsic laryngeal muscles, not the conventional fourth arch branch.
notes.B: The pharyngeal plexus contributes innervation to several fourth arch muscles, but the classic named laryngeal branch is superior laryngeal.
notes.C: The auricular vagal branch supplies selected external ear sensory territories, rather than the characteristic fourth arch muscular derivative.
notes.D: Chorda tympani belongs to the facial nerve and carries taste and parasympathetic fibres, not fourth arch vagal innervation.

questions.stem: The sixth pharyngeal arch is supplied by the
questions.why: The recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles derived from the sixth pharyngeal arch. Its recurrent course reflects remodelling of the embryonic aortic arch arteries.
