notes.B: Superior laryngeal innervation is conventionally associated with fourth arch derivatives, especially the cricothyroid muscle.
notes.C: Glossopharyngeal innervation is associated with third arch derivatives, including the stylopharyngeus muscle rather than intrinsic laryngeal muscles.
notes.D: The facial nerve supplies second arch derivatives, including facial expression muscles rather than sixth arch musculature.
notes.E: The mandibular nerve supplies first arch muscles including mastication muscles, not sixth arch laryngeal derivatives.

questions.stem: Meckel's cartilage, the cartilage of the first arch, gives rise to two ear ossicles, namely the
questions.why: In classical embryology, the dorsal first arch cartilage, called Meckel's cartilage, contributes to development of the malleus and incus. The stapes is associated predominantly with second arch development.

notes.A: The malleus is one first arch ossicle, but the incus is also associated with this arch.
notes.C: The incus is a first arch derivative, whereas the stapes is predominantly associated with the second arch.
notes.D: Malleus and stapes belong to different conventional arch groups, first and second respectively, rather than both first.
notes.E: The stapes is chiefly associated with second arch cartilage rather than the first arch Meckel's cartilage.

questions.stem: Besides the malleus and incus, Meckel's cartilage also gives rise to the
questions.why: Meckel's cartilage largely regresses as the mandible develops around it, but its perichondrial derivatives include the sphenomandibular ligament. The malleus and incus are other classical first arch skeletal derivatives.

notes.A: The greater horn of the hyoid develops from third arch cartilage rather than first arch cartilage.
notes.B: Cricoid cartilage develops from laryngeal mesenchyme associated with fourth and sixth arches rather than Meckel's cartilage.
notes.D: The stylohyoid ligament derives from second arch Reichert's cartilage rather than the cartilage of the first arch.
notes.E: Thyroid cartilage develops within laryngeal mesenchyme associated with later arches, not from Meckel's cartilage.

questions.stem: The stapes, styloid process and upper part of the body of the hyoid are derived from the cartilage of the
questions.why: Reichert's cartilage of the second pharyngeal arch contributes to the stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, lesser hyoid horn and upper hyoid body. These derivatives retain their common developmental arch association.

notes.A: Third arch cartilage contributes the greater hyoid horns and lower body rather than the listed structures.
notes.B: Fourth arch mesenchyme contributes laryngeal cartilages rather than the classic derivatives of second arch Reichert's cartilage.
notes.C: Sixth arch mesenchyme contributes laryngeal structures rather than the styloid process or upper hyoid body.
notes.E: First arch cartilage contributes the malleus, incus and sphenomandibular ligament rather than this second arch combination.

questions.stem: The greater cornu and lower part of the body of the hyoid bone develop from the
questions.why: Third arch cartilage contributes the greater horns and inferior portion of the hyoid body. Second arch cartilage contributes the lesser horns and upper body, accounting for the hyoid's composite embryological origin.

notes.A: Second arch cartilage forms the lesser horns and upper hyoid body rather than the greater horns.
notes.B: First arch cartilage contributes middle ear ossicles and associated ligaments rather than these hyoid components.
notes.C: Fourth arch mesenchyme participates in laryngeal cartilage formation rather than the greater hyoid horn.
notes.D: Sixth arch mesenchyme contributes to laryngeal cartilages rather than the lower body of the hyoid.

questions.stem: The cartilages of the larynx develop from the mesenchyme of the
questions.why: Laryngeal cartilages develop from mesenchymal populations associated with the fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches. Their associated musculature retains vagal innervation, although the precise cellular origins of individual cartilages are more complex.

notes.B: The first and second arches principally contribute craniofacial and hyoid skeletal derivatives rather than the laryngeal cartilage framework.
notes.C: Second and third arch cartilages contribute substantially to the hyoid apparatus rather than the principal laryngeal cartilages.
notes.D: Third arch cartilage contributes hyoid structures, whereas fourth and sixth arch mesenchyme contributes the laryngeal framework.
notes.E: First and third arch derivatives include mandibular-associated structures and portions of the hyoid, not the laryngeal cartilage group.

questions.stem: The muscles of mastication are derived from the
questions.why: Muscles of mastication arise from mesodermal muscle precursors associated with the first pharyngeal arch. Their motor supply remains the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve as the muscles differentiate around the developing jaw.

notes.A: Sixth arch musculature includes most intrinsic laryngeal muscles rather than the skeletal muscles that move the mandible.
notes.C: Second arch musculature forms facial expression muscles supplied by the facial nerve, not the main mastication muscles.
notes.D: Third arch musculature forms stylopharyngeus, rather than the masseter, temporalis and pterygoid muscles of mastication.
notes.E: Fourth arch musculature contributes pharyngeal and cricothyroid muscles rather than the trigeminally innervated mastication muscles.

questions.stem: The muscles of facial expression are derived from the
questions.why: Second arch muscle precursors give rise to muscles of facial expression and several other muscles including stapedius and stylohyoid. Their motor supply remains associated with the facial nerve during migration and differentiation.

notes.A: Fourth arch musculature contributes pharyngeal muscles and cricothyroid, rather than the main facial expression muscle population.
notes.B: Sixth arch derivatives include most intrinsic laryngeal muscles and receive vagal rather than facial motor innervation.
notes.D: First arch muscles include mastication muscles supplied by the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve rather than facial expression muscles.
notes.E: Third arch musculature principally produces stylopharyngeus supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, not facial expression muscles.

questions.stem: The stylopharyngeus muscle is the sole muscle derived from the
questions.why: Stylopharyngeus is the characteristic skeletal muscle derivative of the third pharyngeal arch. Its motor supply from the glossopharyngeal nerve distinguishes it from most other pharyngeal muscles, which receive vagal innervation.

notes.A: First arch muscles include the muscles of mastication and tensor veli palatini rather than stylopharyngeus.
notes.B: Fourth arch derivatives include pharyngeal constrictors and cricothyroid, which differ in developmental nerve association from stylopharyngeus.
notes.C: Sixth arch muscle precursors contribute most intrinsic laryngeal muscles rather than the glossopharyngeally innervated stylopharyngeus.
notes.E: Second arch muscles include facial expression muscles, stylohyoid and stapedius rather than the third arch stylopharyngeus.

questions.stem: Which muscle, derived from the first arch, is innervated by the mandibular nerve and tenses the soft palate?
questions.why: Tensor veli palatini is a first arch muscle supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. It tenses the soft palate and assists opening of the pharyngotympanic tube during swallowing.

notes.A: Levator veli palatini elevates the soft palate and receives vagal innervation through the pharyngeal plexus.
notes.B: Stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx and is a third arch muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
notes.C: Palatoglossus elevates the posterior tongue or lowers the soft palate and is supplied through vagal pathways.
notes.D: Musculus uvulae modifies uvular shape and receives vagal motor supply rather than first arch mandibular innervation.

questions.stem: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx are derived from the
questions.why: The 6th arch forms the intrinsic laryngeal muscles; the 4th arch forms cricothyroid, levator veli palatini and the pharyngeal constrictors.

questions.stem: The first pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the auditory (Eustachian) tube and the
questions.why: The first pharyngeal pouch expands as the tubotympanic recess, whose distal portion forms the epithelial lining of the tympanic cavity. Its proximal portion forms the pharyngotympanic tube connecting middle ear and nasopharynx.

notes.A: The thyroid follicular primordium develops from median pharyngeal endoderm, not the first pouch tubotympanic recess.
notes.C: Palatine tonsillar epithelium derives from the second pouch rather than the first pouch middle ear recess.
notes.D: Inferior parathyroid glands develop from the dorsal third pouch rather than the first pouch.
notes.E: Thymic epithelial tissue develops from the ventral third pouch rather than the tubotympanic recess.

questions.stem: The palatine tonsil develops from the
questions.why: The second pharyngeal pouch endoderm contributes the epithelial lining and crypts of the palatine tonsil. Surrounding mesenchyme subsequently becomes infiltrated by lymphocytes, establishing the characteristic mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.

notes.A: Fourth pouch derivatives include superior parathyroid tissue and associated ultimobranchial structures rather than palatine tonsillar epithelium.
notes.B: The first cleft forms the external acoustic meatus rather than the endodermal epithelium of palatine tonsils.
notes.D: The first pouch contributes the auditory tube and middle ear cavity rather than the tonsillar crypt lining.
notes.E: The third pouch contributes thymic epithelial tissue and inferior parathyroids rather than palatine tonsillar epithelium.

questions.stem: The inferior parathyroid gland and the thymus both develop from the
questions.why: The dorsal wing of the third pharyngeal pouch forms inferior parathyroid primordia, while its ventral wing forms thymic epithelium. Their associated caudal migration explains why third pouch parathyroids ultimately lie below fourth pouch derivatives.

notes.A: The second pouch contributes palatine tonsillar epithelium rather than both thymic and inferior parathyroid primordia.
notes.B: The first pouch forms the tubotympanic recess and does not generate the thymus or inferior parathyroids.
notes.C: The rudimentary fifth pouch is conventionally associated with ultimobranchial tissue rather than these two third pouch derivatives.
notes.E: The fourth pouch contributes superior parathyroids, while thymus and inferior parathyroids originate from the third pouch.

questions.stem: The superior parathyroid gland develops from the dorsal part of the
questions.why: Superior parathyroid glands arise from the dorsal wing of the fourth pharyngeal pouch. They migrate a shorter distance than the third pouch-derived inferior glands and usually settle on the posterior thyroid surface.

notes.A: Third pouch dorsal wings form inferior parathyroids that descend farther with the developing thymic primordia.
notes.B: The second pouch forms palatine tonsillar epithelium, rather than either pair of parathyroid primordia.
notes.C: The first pouch contributes middle ear and auditory tube epithelium rather than superior parathyroid tissue.
notes.D: The rudimentary fifth pouch designation refers to ultimobranchial development rather than the dorsal superior parathyroid primordium.

questions.stem: The inferior parathyroid comes to lie BELOW the superior parathyroid because it
questions.why: Inferior parathyroid primordia arise dorsally from the third pouch and migrate caudally in association with thymic primordia. This longer descent places them below the superior parathyroid glands derived from the fourth pouch.

notes.B: Upward migration would not account for the inferior gland's final position below its fourth pouch counterpart.
notes.C: Inferior parathyroids detach from their pharyngeal origins and migrate caudally rather than remaining within the pharynx.
notes.D: Fourth pouch origin characterises superior parathyroid glands, rather than the inferior glands accompanying thymic descent.
notes.E: Inferior parathyroids settle near the thyroid but do not need to fuse with thyroid tissue to descend.

questions.stem: The parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid are derived from the ultimobranchial body, formed from the
questions.why: The ultimobranchial body contributes calcitonin-producing thyroid parafollicular cells. It is classically described as arising from a rudimentary fifth pharyngeal pouch, often considered part of the ventral fourth pouch in modern accounts.

notes.A: First arch mesenchyme contributes craniofacial structures rather than the endodermal ultimobranchial thyroid cell population.
notes.C: Third pouch endoderm forms thymic epithelium and inferior parathyroids rather than the ultimobranchial body.
notes.D: First pouch endoderm contributes auditory tube and middle ear epithelium rather than parafollicular thyroid cells.
notes.E: The second cleft is external ectoderm rather than the pharyngeal endodermal source of ultimobranchial tissue.

questions.stem: The first pharyngeal cleft (groove) persists in the adult as the
questions.why: The first pharyngeal cleft persists as the external acoustic meatus, lined by ectoderm-derived epithelium. Its deepest part participates in the external epithelial component of the developing tympanic membrane.

notes.A: The cervical sinus temporarily encloses more caudal clefts rather than being the adult first cleft derivative.
notes.B: The tympanic cavity develops from the endodermal first pouch, rather than the external ectodermal first cleft.
notes.D: The auditory tube arises from the first pouch tubotympanic recess rather than the external acoustic meatus primordium.
notes.E: Palatine tonsillar epithelium derives from the second pouch, rather than the first external pharyngeal cleft.

questions.stem: Overgrowth of the second arch over the third and fourth arches encloses an ectoderm-lined space called the
questions.why: The second pharyngeal arch grows caudally over the third and fourth arch regions, enclosing their external clefts within a transient cervical sinus. Normal obliteration removes this ectoderm-lined space during neck development.

notes.A: Foramen caecum is the median tongue landmark of thyroid development, not the enclosed lateral cervical clefts.
notes.B: A cervical cleft cyst is a potential abnormal remnant of the sinus, rather than its normal embryonic name.
notes.C: Pharyngeal membranes mark ectoderm–endoderm interfaces and do not describe the larger cavity enclosed by second arch overgrowth.
notes.E: Stomodeum forms the primitive oral depression and is not the lateral ectoderm-lined cervical cavity.

questions.stem: A branchial (cervical) cleft cyst results from failure of obliteration of the
questions.why: Persistent remnants of the embryonic cervical sinus can produce lateral cervical cleft cysts or related sinus tracts. The sinus normally disappears following caudal overgrowth of the second pharyngeal arch.

notes.A: Persistence of the thyroglossal duct produces a generally midline neck cyst rather than the classical lateral branchial cyst.
notes.B: First pouch remnants involve structures associated with the auditory tube and middle ear rather than cervical sinus persistence.
notes.C: The oronasal membrane separates early nasal and oral spaces, rather than generating lateral neck cysts.
notes.D: The stomodeum develops into the primitive oral cavity and does not normally give rise to cervical sinus remnants.

questions.stem: The pinna (auricle) forms from six auricular hillocks that arise from the first and
questions.why: The auricle develops from six mesenchymal auricular hillocks around the first pharyngeal cleft. These arise from the first and second arches and remodel extensively as the developing ear changes position.

notes.B: Third arch derivatives include hyoid components and stylopharyngeus rather than the second set of auricular hillocks.
notes.C: Fourth arch mesenchyme contributes laryngeal and pharyngeal structures rather than the auricular hillock population.
notes.D: The fifth arch is absent or rudimentary in standard human descriptions and does not generate auricular hillocks.
notes.E: Sixth arch derivatives include laryngeal structures, rather than the paired first and second arch auricular primordia.

questions.stem: Pierre Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis and cleft palate) is a disorder of the
questions.why: Pierre Robin sequence begins with mandibular hypoplasia, involving a structure derived from first arch mesenchyme. Posterior tongue displacement may obstruct the airway and interfere with palatal shelf elevation, producing a secondary cleft palate.

notes.A: The frontonasal prominence contributes nasal and forehead structures rather than the primary mandibular hypoplasia in this sequence.
notes.C: The second arch contributes facial musculature and hyoid-related structures rather than the mandibular skeletal primordium.
notes.D: Third pouch endoderm contributes thymus and inferior parathyroids, not the underdeveloped mandible initiating this sequence.
notes.E: The first cleft contributes external ear canal epithelium rather than the skeletal mandibular abnormality.

questions.stem: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) is characterised by
questions.why: Treacher Collins syndrome is a craniofacial developmental disorder involving abnormalities of neural crest-derived structures, especially mandibular and zygomatic hypoplasia. External and middle ear anomalies may accompany characteristic facial underdevelopment.

notes.A: A protruding tongue can accompany other disorders but does not define mandibulofacial dysostosis with ear anomalies.
notes.B: Premature cranial suture fusion defines craniosynostosis rather than the characteristic mandibulofacial hypoplasia of Treacher Collins syndrome.
notes.D: A single midline eye may occur in severe holoprosencephaly rather than the typical Treacher Collins phenotype.
notes.E: Congenital absence of the nose is arhinia, rather than the characteristic combination of facial skeletal and ear abnormalities.

questions.stem: Congenital complete absence of the nose is termed
questions.why: Arhinia denotes congenital absence of the external nose, often accompanied by abnormal nasal cavities or related craniofacial structures. It reflects major disruption of nasal development rather than an abnormality restricted to nasal size.

notes.A: Macrostomia describes an excessively wide oral opening, rather than congenital absence of nasal structures.
notes.B: Glossoptosis describes posterior displacement of the tongue, frequently associated with mandibular hypoplasia in Pierre Robin sequence.
notes.C: Micrognathia denotes an abnormally small jaw rather than absence of the external nose.
notes.E: Microtia describes underdevelopment of the external ear, rather than congenital absence of the nose.

questions.stem: The face develops from five facial prominences: a single frontonasal prominence, paired maxillary prominences and paired
questions.why: Five facial prominences surround the developing stomodeum: one frontonasal prominence and paired maxillary and mandibular prominences. Their coordinated growth and merging establish the major facial regions, lips and jaw structures.

notes.A: Nasal placodes develop on the frontonasal prominence but are not one of the five initial facial prominences.
notes.B: Palatal shelves grow later from maxillary prominences rather than constituting paired initial facial prominences.
notes.C: Otic placodes contribute inner ear structures and do not form the paired prominences surrounding the stomodeum.
notes.D: Lens placodes contribute ocular lens development rather than forming the paired lower facial prominences.

questions.stem: The frontonasal prominence gives rise to the forehead and the
questions.why: The frontonasal prominence contributes the forehead and nasal bridge and gives rise to medial and lateral nasal prominences around the nasal placodes. Other facial regions develop through interaction with first arch prominences.

notes.B: Lateral upper lip tissue derives from maxillary prominences rather than the frontonasal prominence itself.
notes.C: The lower jaw develops predominantly from mandibular prominences of the first pharyngeal arch, not the frontonasal region.
notes.D: Cheek development involves maxillary and mandibular prominence tissues rather than the characteristic forehead and nasal bridge derivative.
notes.E: Soft palate develops from secondary palatal shelves arising from maxillary prominences rather than frontonasal prominence tissue.

questions.stem: The medial nasal prominences fuse to form the philtrum of the upper lip and the
questions.why: The paired medial nasal prominences merge to form the intermaxillary segment, which contributes the philtrum, premaxillary region and primary palate. The secondary palate instead develops from lateral shelves of the maxillary prominences.

notes.A: Cheek tissue develops mainly from maxillary and mandibular prominence regions rather than the intermaxillary segment.
notes.C: Secondary palate derives from paired maxillary palatal shelves, rather than the merged medial nasal prominences.
notes.D: Nasal alae develop principally from lateral nasal prominences rather than the paired medial nasal prominences.
notes.E: The lower lip develops from merging mandibular prominences rather than the medial nasal intermaxillary segment.

questions.stem: The alae (sides) of the nose are formed by the
questions.why: Lateral nasal prominences develop beside the nasal pits and contribute the alae of the nose. Medial nasal prominences contribute central nasal and upper lip structures, while maxillary prominences form adjacent facial regions.

notes.A: Mandibular prominences contribute the lower lip and jaw, rather than the lateral external nasal wings.
notes.B: The frontonasal prominence gives rise to nasal prominences, but lateral nasal prominences are the immediate alar precursors.
notes.D: Medial nasal prominences contribute central nasal structures and philtrum rather than the lateral alae.
notes.E: Maxillary prominences contribute lateral upper lip and cheek structures rather than directly forming the nasal alae.

questions.stem: The lateral parts of the upper lip are formed by the
questions.why: The maxillary prominences grow medially and merge with medial nasal prominence tissue during facial development. They form the lateral portions of the upper lip, while the central philtrum derives from the intermaxillary segment.

notes.A: Mandibular prominences contribute the lower lip and lower jaw rather than the lateral upper lip.
notes.B: Lateral nasal prominences contribute the alae of the nose, rather than forming most lateral upper lip tissue.
notes.C: Frontonasal prominence contributes forehead and nasal structures, rather than the immediate lateral upper lip primordia.
notes.E: Medial nasal prominences merge to form the philtrum and primary palate rather than the lateral upper lip.

questions.stem: The lower lip and lower jaw are formed by fusion of the
questions.why: Paired mandibular prominences arise from the first pharyngeal arch and merge at the midline beneath the stomodeum. Their mesenchyme and surface tissues contribute the lower lip, chin and developing mandible.

notes.A: Maxillary prominences contribute upper jaw and lateral upper lip structures, rather than the lower jaw and lip.
notes.B: Medial nasal prominences form the intermaxillary segment and philtrum rather than the mandibular midline.
notes.C: Frontonasal prominence contributes forehead and nasal structures rather than the paired lower facial prominences.
notes.D: Lateral nasal prominences contribute the external nasal alae rather than forming the mandible or lower lip.

questions.stem: A unilateral cleft lip results from failure of fusion between the maxillary prominence and the
questions.why: A typical unilateral cleft lip arises when the maxillary prominence fails to merge normally with the medial nasal prominence on one side. This leaves a discontinuity between lateral upper lip and central intermaxillary tissues.

notes.B: Failure involving the lateral nasal prominence is classically associated with an oblique facial cleft rather than typical cleft lip.
notes.C: Failure of maxillary and mandibular merging can alter the oral commissure rather than producing the typical unilateral upper-lip defect.
notes.D: The frontonasal prominence is an earlier regional precursor, not the specific prominence interface implicated in typical unilateral cleft lip.
notes.E: Palatal shelf fusion defects cause secondary cleft palate rather than directly explaining the specified upper-lip discontinuity.

questions.stem: An oblique facial cleft results from failure of fusion between the maxillary prominence and the
questions.why: An oblique facial cleft can follow abnormal merging of the maxillary and lateral nasal prominences along the nasolacrimal groove. The defect may extend towards the medial orbital region, unlike typical isolated cleft lip.

notes.A: The frontonasal prominence supplies nasal precursors, but the specific cleft follows the maxillary–lateral nasal interface.
notes.C: Failure of maxillary and medial nasal merging produces the typical upper cleft lip pattern rather than an oblique facial cleft.
notes.D: Abnormal maxillary and mandibular merging affects the oral commissure, rather than the nasolacrimal groove region.
notes.E: The paired maxillary prominences do not normally merge directly across the nasal region to create this interface.

questions.stem: Excessive fusion of the maxillary and mandibular prominences at the angle of the mouth produces
questions.why: Excessive merging at the maxillary–mandibular prominence junction can restrict the lateral extent of the developing oral opening, producing microstomia. Insufficient merging at this region instead produces an abnormally wide oral opening.

notes.A: Arhinia describes congenital absence of the nose rather than restriction of the oral opening.
notes.B: Glossoptosis describes posterior displacement of the tongue rather than excessive merging at the oral commissures.
notes.D: Macrostomia denotes an excessively wide oral aperture, the opposite of the narrowing described in this question.
notes.E: Cleft lip typically involves abnormal maxillary–medial nasal merging rather than excessive closure at oral commissures.

questions.stem: The labial frenulum is a midline remnant of the
questions.why: The labiogingival lamina develops as an epithelial ingrowth separating the developing lips and cheeks from the gingiva. Its central residual attachment contributes to the labial frenulum within the oral vestibule.

notes.A: The oronasal membrane temporarily separates nasal and oral regions rather than generating the labial attachment fold.
notes.B: Nasal placodes contribute sensory and epithelial nasal structures, rather than the residual midline oral vestibular attachment.
notes.C: The stomodeal membrane separates primitive oral and pharyngeal cavities early in development, not lip from gingiva.
notes.E: Dental lamina produces tooth buds, whereas the neighbouring labiogingival lamina contributes development of the oral vestibule.

questions.stem: The floor of the stomodeum is initially formed by the oropharyngeal membrane, which breaks down at the end of week
questions.why: The oropharyngeal membrane initially separates the ectoderm-lined stomodeum from endodermal foregut. It normally breaks down around day 26 of development, establishing communication between the primitive oral cavity and pharynx.

notes.A: The second week precedes formation and rupture of the mature oropharyngeal membrane during embryonic folding.
notes.B: The sixth week is later than normal establishment of communication between primitive mouth and foregut.
notes.C: By the eighth week the oral and pharyngeal cavities have already been connected for several weeks.
notes.D: The third week precedes the usual late fourth-week breakdown of the oropharyngeal membrane.

questions.stem: The primary palate is derived from the
questions.why: The intermaxillary segment develops through merging of the medial nasal prominences. Its palatal component forms the primary palate, situated anterior to the incisive foramen and associated with the premaxillary incisor region.

notes.B: Secondary palatal shelves arise from maxillary prominences and form the palate posterior to the incisive foramen.
notes.C: Maxillary prominences contribute secondary palatal shelves rather than directly forming the intermaxillary primary palatal segment.
notes.D: The nasal septum fuses with the developing palate but is not the primary palate's embryonic source.
notes.E: The frontonasal prominence is an earlier precursor of nasal prominences, rather than the immediate intermaxillary palatal derivative.

questions.stem: The secondary palate develops from palatal shelves that grow from the
questions.why: Paired palatal shelves grow medially from the maxillary prominences, initially alongside the developing tongue. They elevate and fuse with each other and the primary palate, forming most of the definitive palate.

notes.A: Lateral nasal prominences contribute nasal alae rather than the bilateral secondary palatal shelves.
notes.C: Medial nasal prominences form the intermaxillary segment and primary palate rather than the secondary shelves.
notes.D: Mandibular prominences contribute the lower jaw and influence tongue position, but do not directly produce palatal shelves.
notes.E: Frontonasal prominence contributes nasal structures and medial nasal precursors, not the immediate secondary palatal shelf mesenchyme.

questions.stem: The primary and secondary palates fuse at the
questions.why: The incisive foramen marks the junction between the primary palate derived from the intermaxillary segment and the secondary palate derived from maxillary shelves. It provides a useful landmark for classifying developmental clefts.

notes.A: Greater palatine foramina transmit neurovascular structures posterolaterally rather than marking the primary–secondary palatal junction.
notes.B: The nasal septum fuses superiorly with the palate but is not the specific junctional foramen.
notes.D: The palatine raphe marks the midline fusion of paired shelves rather than specifically the primary–secondary boundary.
notes.E: Foramen caecum is a tongue landmark related to thyroid origin rather than palatal fusion.

questions.stem: Cleft palate results when the palatal shelves fail to
questions.why: Cleft palate can arise through failure of palatal shelf growth, elevation, contact or fusion. Disruption at any of these coordinated stages can leave persistent communication between oral and nasal cavities.

notes.A: Tongue position can obstruct shelf elevation, but the central defect is failure of the shelves to meet and fuse.
notes.B: Neural crest contributes palatal mesenchyme, but isolated failure of its migration is not the sole cleft palate mechanism.
notes.C: The primary palate derives from the intermaxillary segment, rather than being formed by secondary palatal shelves.
notes.E: Palatal bone ossification occurs after shelf fusion; failure of ossification alone does not define a typical cleft palate.

questions.stem: The flat bones of the cranial vault (frontal, parietal) form by
questions.why: Frontal and parietal bones of the cranial vault form predominantly through intramembranous ossification, with bone differentiating directly within mesenchymal condensations. This contrasts with much of the cranial base, which develops through cartilage intermediates.

notes.A: Endochondral ossification requires a cartilage template and predominates in much of the cranial base rather than cranial vault.
notes.B: Pharyngeal arch cartilages contribute selected craniofacial skeletal structures, rather than forming the flat vault bones by fusion.
notes.C: Neural tube induction establishes neural tissue identity and is not the mechanism of cranial bone mineralisation.
notes.D: Notochord signalling influences axial patterning, rather than directly describing the bone formation process of the cranial vault.

questions.stem: The base of the skull (chondrocranium) is formed by
questions.why: The chondrocranium develops as a cartilaginous framework around the developing brain and sensory structures. Endochondral ossification replaces this cartilage with bone, unlike the predominantly intramembranous development of the cranial vault.

notes.B: Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly within mesenchyme and predominates in the cranial vault rather than the base.
notes.C: Neural crest contributes anterior cranial base mesenchyme, but condensation alone does not describe the ossification mechanism.
notes.D: Occipital somites contribute posterior cranial structures, but their fusion is not the general mechanism of chondrocranial ossification.
notes.E: Placodes contribute sensory structures through epithelial specialisation rather than replacing cranial base cartilage with bone.

questions.stem: The facial skeleton (viscerocranium) is derived mainly from the
questions.why: The viscerocranium develops largely from cranial neural crest mesenchyme associated with the first and second pharyngeal arches, with additional contributions from the frontonasal region. It forms the facial skeletal framework and associated structures.

notes.A: Lateral plate mesoderm contributes other skeletal regions but is not the principal source of the facial skeleton.
notes.C: The frontonasal prominence contributes important facial bones, but it does not alone form the entire viscerocranium.
notes.D: Paraxial mesoderm contributes cranial and axial tissues, but most facial skeletal mesenchyme derives from cranial neural crest.
notes.E: The notochord patterns axial structures and does not itself generate the principal facial skeletal components.

questions.stem: The anterior fontanelle normally closes by about
questions.why: The anterior fontanelle permits skull deformation during birth and accommodates rapid brain growth. It typically closes during the second year of life, with considerable normal variation around the conventional eighteen-month estimate.

notes.A: Closure at three years would be later than the usual teaching estimate, although timing varies between children.
notes.B: The anterior fontanelle normally remains open at birth to accommodate continued expansion of the developing brain.
notes.D: Closure around two months is more characteristic of the smaller posterior fontanelle than the anterior fontanelle.
notes.E: Six months is earlier than the conventional anterior fontanelle closure estimate, although early normal closure can occur.

questions.stem: The mucosa of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue develops from the lateral lingual swellings and the
questions.why: The first arch produces paired lateral lingual swellings and a median tuberculum impar. The lateral swellings enlarge and merge over the median swelling, forming most of the mucosal anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

notes.A: The hypopharyngeal eminence contributes principally to the posterior tongue rather than the anterior first arch region.
notes.B: Foramen caecum marks the embryonic thyroid origin and is not a major anterior lingual swelling.
notes.C: The epiglottic swelling contributes the caudal tongue and epiglottic region rather than the anterior oral tongue.
notes.E: The copula is associated with the second arch and is largely overgrown during posterior tongue development.

questions.stem: General sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the
questions.why: The anterior oral tongue derives mainly from first arch swellings, accounting for its general sensory supply through the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve. Taste fibres travel separately through chorda tympani before joining it.

notes.A: Chorda tympani conveys taste from most of the anterior tongue rather than its principal general sensory supply.
notes.B: Glossopharyngeal fibres convey general sensation and taste chiefly from the posterior third, including circumvallate taste buds.
notes.C: The hypoglossal nerve principally supplies tongue muscles rather than ordinary mucosal sensation from the anterior tongue.
notes.D: Vagal sensory fibres serve the epiglottic and adjacent pharyngeal region rather than most of the oral tongue.

questions.stem: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the
questions.why: Chorda tympani carries taste afferents from most of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and joins the lingual nerve peripherally. Circumvallate papillae are an important glossopharyngeal exception despite their anterior position.

notes.B: The lingual nerve conveys general sensation and carries accompanying chorda tympani fibres, rather than supplying taste independently.
notes.C: Glossopharyngeal taste fibres serve the posterior third and circumvallate papillae, rather than most of the anterior oral tongue.
notes.D: Hypoglossal fibres provide motor innervation to most tongue muscles rather than transporting gustatory afferent information.
notes.E: Vagal taste fibres serve selected epiglottic and pharyngeal regions, rather than most anterior tongue taste buds.

questions.stem: The posterior one-third of the tongue develops mainly from the
questions.why: The third arch component of the hypopharyngeal eminence expands over the second arch copula and contributes most of the posterior third of the tongue. Glossopharyngeal sensory innervation reflects this developmental association.

notes.A: The fourth arch contributes the most caudal tongue and epiglottic region rather than the entire posterior third.
notes.C: First arch lingual swellings contribute most of the anterior oral tongue rather than the posterior pharyngeal portion.
notes.D: The second arch copula is largely overgrown by third arch tissue and does not form the principal posterior mucosa.
notes.E: Occipital somites provide tongue muscle precursors rather than the pharyngeal arch-derived mucosal region specified here.

questions.stem: The intrinsic muscles of the tongue develop from
questions.why: Myogenic precursors migrate from occipital somites into the developing tongue, forming its intrinsic and most extrinsic skeletal muscles. Their hypoglossal motor innervation reflects this migration from the occipital region.

notes.A: Tuberculum impar contributes an early lingual mucosal swelling rather than the migrating skeletal muscle precursor population.
notes.B: Lateral plate mesoderm supplies several other muscular and connective tissues, but tongue myoblasts originate in occipital somites.
notes.D: First arch mesenchyme contributes anterior tongue mucosal structures rather than the principal intrinsic tongue muscle precursors.
notes.E: Neural crest contributes craniofacial connective tissues but does not supply the conventional occipital myogenic population.

questions.stem: All tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve EXCEPT the palatoglossus, which is supplied by the
questions.why: Most tongue muscles arise from occipital somites and receive hypoglossal motor innervation. Palatoglossus is functionally associated with the soft palate and receives vagal motor fibres through the pharyngeal plexus.

notes.A: The facial nerve supplies facial expression and selected second arch muscles rather than motor fibres to palatoglossus.
notes.B: Trigeminal motor fibres supply muscles of mastication and tensor veli palatini, rather than the palatoglossus muscle.
notes.C: Although cranial accessory fibres were historically described in this pathway, palatoglossus is clinically innervated through the vagus.
notes.E: Glossopharyngeal motor fibres supply stylopharyngeus, rather than the palatal muscle that elevates the posterior tongue.

questions.stem: The boundary between the anterior and posterior parts of the tongue is the V-shaped
questions.why: The sulcus terminalis is a V-shaped groove separating the oral anterior two-thirds from the pharyngeal posterior third of the tongue. Its apex contains the foramen caecum, marking the embryonic thyroid origin.

notes.A: The palatine raphe marks midline palatal fusion and is not the boundary between the two tongue regions.
notes.B: The linguogingival region lies between tongue and gingiva, rather than separating oral and pharyngeal tongue surfaces.
notes.C: The median sulcus divides the oral tongue longitudinally rather than marking its posterior transverse developmental boundary.
notes.D: Circumvallate papillae lie just anterior to the sulcus terminalis, but the groove itself defines the boundary.

questions.stem: Failure of the lateral lingual swellings to fuse completely in the midline produces a
questions.why: Incomplete merging of paired lateral lingual swellings can produce a bifid tongue, typically with a midline division. The abnormality reflects disruption of the developmental union that normally establishes a continuous anterior tongue.

notes.B: Tongue-tie involves a restrictive lingual frenulum rather than incomplete midline merging of paired lingual swellings.
notes.C: Macroglossia denotes abnormal enlargement of the tongue and does not specifically describe a developmental midline cleft.
notes.D: Lingual thyroid results from abnormal thyroid descent and is not caused by failure of lingual swelling fusion.
notes.E: Geographic tongue involves migrating areas of papillary loss and inflammation rather than a congenital bifid configuration.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland first develops as a median endodermal thickening at the
questions.why: The thyroid follicular primordium arises as a median thickening of endoderm in the floor of the primitive pharynx. Its original site persists as the foramen caecum at the apex of the sulcus terminalis.

notes.A: The copula contributes an early posterior lingual swelling rather than the median site of thyroid follicular origin.
notes.C: The sulcus terminalis contains the foramen caecum at its apex, which is the more precise thyroid landmark.
notes.D: The incisive foramen marks primary and secondary palate relationships rather than the embryonic site of thyroid origin.
notes.E: The stomodeum is the ectodermal primitive mouth, whereas the thyroid primordium arises from pharyngeal endoderm.

questions.stem: During its descent the thyroid gland remains connected to the tongue by the
questions.why: The thyroid primordium descends from the floor of the primitive pharynx while temporarily retaining a narrow epithelial connection called the thyroglossal duct. This connection normally degenerates as the gland reaches its cervical location.

notes.A: The nasolacrimal duct develops between maxillary and lateral nasal prominences rather than connecting thyroid and tongue.
notes.B: The vitelline duct connects the developing midgut to the yolk sac, not the descending thyroid primordium.
notes.D: Pharyngeal membranes are interfaces between ectoderm and endoderm rather than the epithelial tract accompanying thyroid descent.
notes.E: The cervical sinus encloses lateral pharyngeal clefts temporarily and does not connect the thyroid to the tongue.

questions.stem: The thyroid reaches its final position anterior to the trachea, below the cricoid, by about week
questions.why: The thyroid primordium descends anterior to the developing pharyngeal and laryngeal structures and normally reaches its pretracheal position by approximately the seventh embryonic week. Subsequent differentiation establishes mature follicular organisation and function.

notes.A: Ten weeks is later than the conventional completion of thyroid descent, although glandular differentiation continues afterwards.
notes.B: Twelve weeks relates more closely to developing thyroid functional maturation than to reaching the definitive cervical position.
notes.C: Sixteen weeks is well after normal anatomical thyroid descent has been completed during the embryonic period.
notes.E: The fourth week marks early formation of the thyroid primordium rather than completion of its cervical descent.

questions.stem: A thyroid that fails to descend and remains at the back of the tongue is a
questions.why: Failure or interruption of normal thyroid descent can leave functioning ectopic thyroid tissue near the foramen caecum at the tongue base. This lingual thyroid may represent the individual's only functional thyroid tissue.

notes.A: A thyroglossal cyst forms from residual duct tissue and does not necessarily contain an entire ectopic thyroid gland.
notes.B: A pyramidal lobe is a superior extension of thyroid tissue associated with duct remnants, not a lingual gland.
notes.C: Ectopic parathyroids arise from altered pharyngeal pouch migration rather than failure of median thyroid primordium descent.
notes.D: The tubercle of Zuckerkandl is a posterior thyroid projection rather than thyroid tissue retained at the tongue base.

questions.stem: A persistent remnant of the thyroglossal duct that accumulates fluid in the midline neck is a
questions.why: A thyroglossal duct cyst develops when epithelial remnants of the transient thyroid descent tract persist and accumulate fluid. It commonly presents as a midline cervical lesion near the hyoid and may move with swallowing.

notes.B: Branchial cleft cysts usually occur laterally and arise from developmental remnants associated with pharyngeal cleft structures.
notes.C: Dermoid cysts contain ectodermal elements and may occur in the midline, but do not specifically arise from thyroglossal duct remnants.
notes.D: Cystic hygroma is a lymphatic malformation rather than an epithelial cyst arising along the thyroid descent pathway.
notes.E: A ranula arises from salivary mucus accumulation, usually involving the sublingual gland rather than a thyroglossal duct remnant.

questions.stem: Tooth development (odontogenesis) results from interaction between oral ectoderm and mesenchyme derived from
questions.why: Tooth development depends on reciprocal signalling between oral ectoderm and neural crest-derived ectomesenchyme. The epithelial component produces enamel-forming ameloblasts, while mesenchymal derivatives contribute dentin, pulp and the supporting periodontal tissues.

notes.A: Paraxial mesoderm contributes craniofacial muscles, but dental ectomesenchyme derives principally from migrating cranial neural crest cells.
notes.C: Occipital somites contribute tongue muscle precursors rather than the principal connective-tissue precursors involved in odontogenesis.
notes.D: Lateral plate mesoderm forms many other skeletal and connective tissues but is not the main dental mesenchymal source.
notes.E: Endoderm lines portions of the primitive gut and does not provide the characteristic neural crest-derived dental ectomesenchyme.

questions.stem: The enamel organ, which gives rise to ameloblasts, is derived from
questions.why: The dental lamina arises from oral ectoderm and gives rise to the epithelial enamel organ. Inner enamel epithelial cells differentiate into ameloblasts that synthesise enamel matrix following inductive interactions with dental papilla mesenchyme.

notes.A: The dental follicle is mesenchymal and contributes supporting periodontal tissues rather than the epithelial enamel organ.
notes.B: Endoderm contributes pharyngeal and gut epithelial structures, rather than the oral ectodermal enamel-forming epithelium.
notes.D: Neural crest-derived mesenchyme forms the dental papilla and follicle, not the epithelial cells producing enamel.
notes.E: Dental papilla supplies odontoblasts and pulp cells rather than the enamel organ's ameloblast lineage.

questions.stem: Dentine and the dental pulp are formed from the
questions.why: The dental papilla consists of neural crest-derived ectomesenchyme within the concavity of the enamel organ. Peripheral papilla cells differentiate into dentin-producing odontoblasts, while its remaining central tissue becomes dental pulp.

notes.A: Dental follicle contributes cementum and periodontal supporting tissues, rather than the internal dentin and pulp components.
notes.B: Dental lamina is an epithelial structure giving rise to tooth buds, not the mesenchymal dental papilla.
notes.C: Stellate reticulum is part of the epithelial enamel organ and does not generate odontoblasts or pulp connective tissue.
notes.E: The enamel organ produces ameloblasts and associated epithelial structures rather than the mesenchymal dental pulp and dentin.

questions.stem: Cementum, the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone all develop from the
questions.why: The dental follicle surrounds the developing enamel organ and dental papilla as ectomesenchymal tissue. Its cells contribute cementoblasts, periodontal ligament fibroblasts and osteoblasts associated with supporting alveolar bone during tooth development.

notes.A: Dental papilla contributes dentin-producing odontoblasts and pulp connective tissue, rather than the external supporting periodontal structures.
notes.B: The enamel organ provides epithelial ameloblasts for enamel production, rather than the mesenchymal periodontal supporting tissues.
notes.C: Inner enamel epithelium differentiates into ameloblasts and does not directly generate cementoblasts or ligament fibroblasts.
notes.D: Dental lamina initiates epithelial tooth buds, rather than forming the surrounding mesenchymal follicular supporting tissue.

questions.stem: Enamel cannot be regenerated after tooth eruption because
questions.why: Ameloblasts deposit enamel before eruption but are lost from the tooth surface during eruption. Mature enamel therefore lacks cells capable of secreting replacement enamel matrix, although limited mineral remineralisation can still occur.

notes.B: Dentin lies beneath enamel and does not prevent regeneration by covering the erupted enamel surface.
notes.C: Odontoblasts persist at the pulp–dentin interface and can produce additional dentin, rather than being lost with ameloblasts.
notes.D: Dental pulp normally remains viable after eruption and does not explain the absence of enamel-forming cells.
notes.E: Cementum covers the root and does not normally replace crown enamel following the eruption of a tooth.

questions.stem: The deciduous (primary) dentition consists of how many teeth?
questions.why: The primary dentition comprises twenty teeth, with two incisors, one canine and two molars in each quadrant. These teeth are progressively replaced by permanent successors during childhood, with permanent molars erupting posteriorly.

notes.A: Twenty-eight describes permanent dentition when third molars are excluded, rather than the number of primary teeth.
notes.C: Thirty-two is the conventional complete adult permanent dentition including third molars, not the deciduous set.
notes.D: Sixteen would omit four teeth from the normal primary dentition of five teeth per quadrant.
notes.E: Twenty-four exceeds the usual primary tooth number, which contains no premolars and only two molars per quadrant.

questions.stem: Which stage of tooth development shows the enamel organ with a dental papilla and dental follicle first recognisable?
questions.why: During the cap stage, the epithelial tooth bud develops a concave enamel organ over a condensed dental papilla. The surrounding dental follicle becomes distinguishable, establishing the three major components of the developing tooth germ.

notes.A: Initiation establishes dental lamina before the three distinct morphological components of the tooth germ become recognisable.
notes.B: Maturation involves later differentiation and mineralisation rather than initial recognition of the cap-shaped enamel organ.
notes.D: The bud stage forms rounded epithelial ingrowths, preceding the characteristic concavity surrounding the dental papilla.
notes.E: The bell stage follows the cap stage and shows more advanced epithelial differentiation and crown shape specification.

questions.stem: The respiratory primordium first appears in week 4 as the
questions.why: The respiratory primordium emerges during the fourth week as a laryngotracheal groove in ventral foregut endoderm. This deepens and develops into a respiratory diverticulum that subsequently produces the developing lung buds.

notes.B: Bronchial buds emerge as the respiratory diverticulum branches, rather than being the earliest ventral foregut groove.
notes.C: Septum transversum contributes to diaphragm and liver-associated structures rather than the initial respiratory epithelial primordium.
notes.D: Pleuropericardial folds separate developing thoracic cavities and arise after the initial respiratory primordium appears.
notes.E: The cloacal membrane marks the caudal digestive and urogenital region rather than the cranial foregut respiratory origin.

questions.stem: The laryngotracheal tube is separated from the oesophagus by the
questions.why: The respiratory diverticulum separates from the dorsal foregut as the tracheoesophageal region undergoes coordinated remodelling. The resulting tracheoesophageal septum conventionally describes the partition between the ventral respiratory tube and dorsal oesophagus.

notes.A: The dorsal mesentery suspends portions of the digestive tract and does not form the tracheoesophageal partition.
notes.C: The urorectal septum divides the cloacal region into anorectal and urogenital compartments rather than separating respiratory and oesophageal tubes.
notes.D: The laryngeal inlet maintains communication with the pharynx rather than constituting the septum separating the two tubes.
notes.E: Pleuroperitoneal membranes contribute to diaphragm development and closure of thoracoabdominal communications, not foregut tube partitioning.

questions.stem: The epithelium lining the trachea, bronchi and alveoli is derived from
questions.why: The epithelial lining of the lower respiratory tract develops from the endoderm of the ventral foregut diverticulum. Its descendants differentiate into conducting airway epithelial cells and alveolar epithelial populations specialised for gas exchange.

notes.A: Somatic mesoderm contributes parietal body-wall and serosal structures, rather than respiratory epithelial cells arising from foregut.
notes.B: Surface ectoderm contributes other epithelial structures but does not form the lower respiratory endodermal lining.
notes.D: Splanchnic mesoderm contributes respiratory connective tissue, cartilage and smooth muscle rather than the epithelial luminal lining.
notes.E: Neural crest contributes selected peripheral neural and skeletal structures, not the principal epithelium of the lower respiratory tract.

questions.stem: The cartilage and smooth muscle of the respiratory tree are derived from
questions.why: Splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm surrounding the respiratory diverticulum differentiates into smooth muscle, cartilage and connective tissue of the lower respiratory tree. Foregut endoderm instead produces the specialised epithelial lining of these structures.

notes.A: Neural crest contributes selected craniofacial and laryngeal structures, but the lower airway supporting tissue chiefly derives from splanchnic mesoderm.
notes.B: Surface ectoderm is not the mesenchymal source of lower airway cartilage and smooth muscle surrounding the respiratory diverticulum.
notes.C: The notochord provides axial patterning signals and does not directly form the structural mesenchyme of the respiratory tree.
notes.E: Foregut endoderm produces airway epithelium rather than the surrounding cartilage and smooth-muscle components.

questions.stem: An incompletely formed tracheoesophageal septum results in a
questions.why: Abnormal separation of the ventral respiratory tube from the dorsal oesophagus may leave a tracheoesophageal fistula, often associated with oesophageal atresia. The persistent communication allows passage of fluid or air between the two systems.

notes.A: Diaphragmatic hernia results from abnormal formation of the diaphragm rather than incomplete foregut respiratory and oesophageal separation.
notes.B: Congenital pulmonary cysts involve abnormal airway or lung development rather than the specific persistent communication described here.
notes.C: Congenital lobar overinflation involves abnormal airway mechanics, rather than a direct connection between trachea and oesophagus.
notes.D: Cleft palate results from abnormal palatal shelf development and fusion, not defective respiratory diverticulum partitioning.

questions.stem: Inhaled foreign objects lodge more often in the right main bronchus because it is
questions.why: In adults, the right main bronchus is generally wider, shorter and more vertical than the left. Aspirated material therefore often follows its more direct route, although distribution also depends on body position and age.

notes.B: A longer more horizontal course characterises the left main bronchus rather than the usual right bronchial configuration.
notes.C: The right main bronchus generally has a larger calibre, rather than being narrower than the left.
notes.D: The right main bronchus takes a relatively direct descending course, rather than a sharply medial angled trajectory.
notes.E: Both main bronchi contain cartilaginous support and other wall components, so cartilage alone does not explain aspiration laterality.

questions.stem: During lung development the right lung is supplied by how many lobar (secondary) bronchi?
questions.why: The right primary bronchial bud divides into three secondary bronchi corresponding to the superior, middle and inferior pulmonary lobes. The left primary bronchial bud produces two secondary bronchi for its two lobes.

notes.A: Five is the combined number of conventional lobar bronchi across both lungs, rather than the right lung alone.
notes.C: Two corresponds to the usual number of left lobar bronchi, not the right-sided branching arrangement.
notes.D: Four is not the ordinary number of right lobar bronchi, which correspond to three anatomical pulmonary lobes.
notes.E: One describes the initial right main bronchus before its division into the three secondary lobar branches.

questions.stem: During which phase of lung development does the air-blood barrier first begin to form?
questions.why: During the canalicular stage, distal respiratory epithelium thins and capillaries approach the developing airspaces, initiating formation of a gas-exchange barrier. Subsequent saccular development expands these specialised surfaces and improves potential pulmonary gas exchange.

notes.A: The alveolar stage expands and matures gas-exchange units, rather than being the earliest stage establishing epithelial–capillary proximity.
notes.B: The embryonic phase establishes lung buds and major airways before distal gas-exchange barrier differentiation occurs.
notes.D: The pseudoglandular phase produces conducting airway branching but lacks adequate specialised distal surfaces for gas exchange.
notes.E: The terminal saccular phase further develops thin exchange surfaces that begin forming during the earlier canalicular stage.

questions.stem: Type I pneumocytes (thin squamous cells) first differentiate during the
questions.why: In the saccular phase the epithelium thins into type I pneumocytes, establishing terminal air sacs for gas exchange.

questions.stem: Surfactant-producing type II pneumocytes begin to differentiate from about
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes appear from about 28 weeks; a baby born at 28 weeks has a chance of surviving unaided.

questions.stem: Respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease) of the newborn is caused by
questions.why: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome results principally from insufficient pulmonary surfactant, especially in preterm infants. Elevated surface tension promotes alveolar collapse, reduced compliance and hypoxaemia, with proteinaceous hyaline membranes developing in injured airspaces.

notes.B: Excess amniotic fluid may accompany selected fetal disorders, but it is not the primary cause of surfactant-deficient respiratory distress.
notes.C: Failure of bronchial branching can cause pulmonary hypoplasia, rather than the characteristic surfactant deficiency of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
notes.D: Tracheoesophageal fistula causes abnormal airway–oesophageal communication and aspiration risk, not the primary alveolar surface-tension defect.
notes.E: Diaphragmatic herniation may impair lung growth but is a distinct developmental cause of respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: Before birth, gas exchange for the fetus is carried out by the
questions.why: Before birth, placental chorionic villi provide the interface for oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide transfer between maternal and fetal circulations. Fetal lungs are fluid-filled and receive limited blood flow, rather than providing air-based gas exchange.

notes.A: The fetal liver supports metabolism and haematopoiesis but does not exchange respiratory gases directly with maternal blood.
notes.C: Fetal lungs develop and perform breathing movements but do not provide effective air-based gas exchange before birth.
notes.D: Amniotic fluid surrounds and protects the fetus, rather than serving as its principal respiratory gas-exchange interface.
notes.E: The ductus arteriosus redirects blood away from fetal lungs but does not itself exchange gases with maternal blood.

questions.stem: A markedly reduced volume of amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios) is associated with
questions.why: Prolonged severe oligohydramnios can restrict normal fetal lung expansion and alter thoracic development. Reduced growth of respiratory airways and exchange tissues may produce pulmonary hypoplasia, especially when fluid loss occurs early in gestation.

notes.A: Congenital lung cysts arise from abnormal respiratory development rather than representing the characteristic consequence of reduced amniotic fluid.
notes.B: Diaphragmatic hernia may independently cause pulmonary hypoplasia through compression, but it is not the defining consequence of oligohydramnios.
notes.D: Congenital lobar overinflation involves airway mechanics and is not the characteristic outcome of impaired fetal lung expansion.
notes.E: Tracheoesophageal fistula results from abnormal foregut separation rather than reduced amniotic fluid volume itself.

questions.stem: Fetal breathing movements, which condition the respiratory muscles, begin at about
questions.why: Rhythmic fetal breathing movements using amniotic fluid are seen from about 20-21 weeks.

questions.stem: The embryonic body cavities all arise from the
questions.why: The intraembryonic coelom develops within lateral plate mesoderm and initially forms a horseshoe-shaped cavity. Embryonic folding and subsequent partitioning produce the pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities from this common developmental space.

notes.A: The amniotic cavity surrounds the embryo externally and does not form the internal serous body cavities.
notes.B: The extraembryonic coelom surrounds the early embryonic structures, whereas internal body cavities develop from the intraembryonic coelom.
notes.C: The neural tube encloses the developing central nervous system canal rather than the body's serous cavities.
notes.D: The yolk sac contributes early nutritional and developmental functions but does not form the internal pleural and peritoneal spaces.

questions.stem: Cavitation of the lateral plate mesoderm splits it into a somatic layer and a
questions.why: Cavities within lateral plate mesoderm coalesce into the intraembryonic coelom, separating somatic mesoderm adjacent to ectoderm from splanchnic mesoderm adjacent to endoderm. Their derivatives support body walls and developing viscera respectively.

notes.B: Paraxial mesoderm lies closer to the neural axis and forms somites rather than being a leaflet of lateral plate.
notes.C: Intermediate mesoderm lies between paraxial and lateral plate regions and contributes urogenital development rather than coelomic leaflets.
notes.D: Notochordal tissue forms the axial midline rather than one of the layers produced by lateral plate cavitation.
notes.E: The conventional paired layer names are somatic and splanchnic, rather than somatic and a nonspecific dorsal layer.

questions.stem: The pleural and pericardial cavities are separated from each other by the
questions.why: Pleuropericardial folds grow into the developing thoracic coelomic spaces and separate pleural cavities from the pericardial cavity. Their membranes contribute to the fibrous pericardium and carry developing phrenic nerves during this process.

notes.A: The urorectal septum partitions the cloaca into digestive and urogenital regions rather than separating thoracic serous cavities.
notes.C: Pleuroperitoneal folds close communications between pleural and peritoneal cavities, not between pleural and pericardial cavities.
notes.D: Septum transversum contributes to the diaphragm's central tendon and does not principally partition the cardiac and pulmonary cavities.
notes.E: Dorsal mesenteric tissue contributes organ suspension and selected diaphragm components rather than the pleuropericardial partition.

questions.stem: The pleuropericardial folds carry which two structures?

options.label: B
options.text: the splanchnic nerves and the SMA

options.label: D
options.text: the vagus nerve and the aorta

options.label: E
options.text: the thoracic duct and azygos vein

questions.why: Developing pleuropericardial folds contain the common cardinal veins and phrenic nerves as they project into the thoracic coelom. Their subsequent fusion partitions the pericardial and pleural cavities and establishes the phrenic nerve relationship.

notes.A: The oesophagus and trachea develop from foregut structures rather than passing within the pleuropericardial folds.
notes.B: Splanchnic nerves and the superior mesenteric artery are associated with abdominal structures, not the thoracic folds.
notes.D: The vagus and aorta have important mediastinal relationships but are not the characteristic pair contained in these folds.
notes.E: The thoracic duct and azygos vein develop from other vascular and lymphatic pathways rather than the characteristic fold contents.

questions.stem: The fused pleuropericardial membranes form the
questions.why: The pleuropericardial membranes fuse and separate the pericardial cavity from the developing pleural cavities. Their connective tissue contributes to the fibrous pericardium, explaining the close association of the phrenic nerves with its lateral surfaces.

notes.A: Mediastinal pleura is parietal serosa derived from somatic mesoderm rather than the specified fibrous membrane derivative.
notes.B: Serous pericardium develops from coelomic lining, whereas the folds principally contribute to the fibrous pericardium.
notes.C: The transverse pericardial sinus results from cardiac tube and mesocardial remodelling rather than membrane fusion.
notes.E: The central tendon derives classically from septum transversum, rather than the pleuropericardial membranes.

questions.stem: The right pleuropericardial opening closes before the left because

options.label: B
options.text: the heart descends to the left

options.label: C
options.text: the right phrenic nerve is shorter

options.label: D
options.text: the left horn forms the coronary sinus

options.label: E
options.text: the right common cardinal vein is larger

questions.why: The larger right common cardinal vein produces a larger membrane, so the right canal closes first.

questions.stem: The central tendon of the diaphragm is derived from the
questions.why: Septum transversum is a mesodermal mass that initially separates parts of the thoracic and abdominal coelom. Its major classical diaphragmatic derivative is the central tendon, subsequently joined by other developing diaphragm components.

notes.B: Pleuroperitoneal membranes close the posterolateral canals and contribute to the developing diaphragm rather than specifically its central tendon.
notes.C: Dorsal oesophageal mesentery contributes the crural region around the oesophageal hiatus rather than the central tendon.
notes.D: Cervical myotomes supply migrating diaphragm muscle precursors, rather than forming the principal central tendinous component.
notes.E: The lateral body wall contributes peripheral diaphragmatic tissue and musculature, not the classical septum transversum-derived tendon.

questions.stem: The crura of the diaphragm develop from the
questions.why: The dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus contributes to development of the diaphragmatic crura surrounding the oesophageal hiatus. These muscular structures anchor the diaphragm posteriorly and help support the oesophageal opening.

notes.A: The yolk sac contributes primitive gut endoderm and early embryonic functions rather than the diaphragmatic crura.
notes.C: Septum transversum provides the classical central tendon component rather than the oesophageal mesentery-derived crural region.
notes.D: Pleuropericardial folds contribute fibrous pericardium and do not form the crura surrounding the oesophagus.
notes.E: The lateral body wall contributes peripheral diaphragm components, rather than the specific dorsal mesenteric contribution.

questions.stem: The muscle of the diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, reflecting its origin from myotomes of segments
questions.why: Diaphragmatic muscle precursors originate predominantly from cervical somites associated with segments C3–C5. The phrenic nerves accompany their migration during diaphragm descent, preserving cervical motor innervation despite the adult muscle's thoracoabdominal position.

notes.A: Upper thoracic segments supply other thoracic structures, rather than the characteristic phrenic nerve cervical root values.
notes.B: Upper lumbar segments contribute to lumbar plexus innervation rather than the phrenic motor supply to diaphragm.
notes.D: Lower thoracic nerves innervate abdominal wall and peripheral sensory territories but do not provide the principal diaphragmatic motor supply.
notes.E: The first two cervical segments are above the conventional root levels contributing to the phrenic nerves.

questions.stem: The pleural and peritoneal cavities are separated by the
questions.why: Pleuroperitoneal membranes grow to close the transient pericardioperitoneal canals between thoracic and abdominal coelomic spaces. Together with septum transversum and other tissue contributions, they establish the developing diaphragm and separate these cavities.

notes.A: Septum transversum initially incompletely partitions the coelom and requires additional components to close the posterolateral communications.
notes.B: The urorectal septum separates cloacal urogenital and anorectal regions rather than thoracic and abdominal cavities.
notes.C: The oropharyngeal membrane separates primitive oral cavity and foregut, rather than closing coelomic communications.
notes.E: Pleuropericardial folds separate pleural and pericardial cavities rather than the pleural and peritoneal compartments.

questions.stem: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia most often occurs on the left posterolateral side because

options.label: A
options.text: the liver blocks the right side

options.label: C
options.text: the stomach is on the left

questions.why: The left pleuroperitoneal canal (foramen of Bochdalek) closes later than the right, so herniation is commoner on the left.

questions.stem: The lung on the side of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia characteristically shows
questions.why: A congenital diaphragmatic hernia can permit abdominal viscera to occupy the developing thorax and compress the lungs. Restricted pulmonary growth produces hypoplasia, often involving both lungs but typically more severe ipsilateral to the defect.

notes.B: Lobar emphysema involves abnormal air trapping and distension rather than reduced development from fetal thoracic compression.
notes.C: Surfactant production can be impaired in hypoplastic lungs; excessive surfactant is not the characteristic structural abnormality.
notes.D: Congenital pulmonary cysts arise from other developmental abnormalities, rather than being the usual consequence of diaphragmatic herniation.
notes.E: Tracheoesophageal fistula reflects abnormal foregut separation and does not explain the lung growth restriction caused by herniation.

questions.stem: The primitive gut tube is formed from the
questions.why: Cranial, caudal and lateral embryonic folding incorporate part of the yolk sac endoderm into the embryo as the primitive gut tube. The remaining extraembryonic yolk sac temporarily communicates with the midgut.

notes.B: The amniotic cavity surrounds the embryo and does not supply the endodermal lining of the primitive intestine.
notes.C: The allantois extends from the caudal yolk sac region but does not form the entire gut tube.
notes.D: The notochord establishes axial patterning and provides inductive signals rather than generating gut endoderm.
notes.E: The neural tube develops from neuroectoderm and forms the central nervous system, not the primitive alimentary tube.

questions.stem: The cranial limit of the foregut is marked by the
questions.why: The buccopharyngeal or oropharyngeal membrane marks the cranial end of the primitive foregut, separating it from the stomodeum. Its rupture establishes continuity between the developing mouth and pharynx during early development.

notes.A: The urorectal septum partitions the caudal cloaca rather than marking the cranial end of the foregut.
notes.C: The cloacal membrane marks the caudal termination of the embryonic gut rather than its cranial boundary.
notes.D: The standard structure at this boundary is a bilaminar membrane, rather than a separate oropharyngeal septum.
notes.E: The vitelline duct connects the developing midgut with the extraembryonic yolk sac, not the cranial foregut.

questions.stem: The artery of the midgut is the
questions.why: The superior mesenteric artery supplies derivatives of the embryonic midgut, extending from the distal duodenum to approximately the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. Midgut rotation occurs around this arterial axis.

notes.A: The splenic artery branches from the coeliac trunk and supplies foregut-associated organs rather than the entire midgut.
notes.B: The hepatic artery supplies the liver and other foregut-associated structures, not the principal midgut arterial territory.
notes.D: The coeliac trunk supplies foregut derivatives, contrasting with the superior mesenteric supply of the midgut.
notes.E: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut derivatives rather than the embryonic midgut and its principal branches.

questions.stem: The muscle in the upper third of the oesophagus is
questions.why: The proximal third of the mature oesophagus contains predominantly striated skeletal muscle in its muscularis externa. The middle third contains mixed muscle types, whereas the distal third is predominantly smooth muscle.

notes.A: The mixed arrangement characterises the middle oesophageal third rather than the predominantly striated upper third.
notes.B: Cardiac muscle is specialised myocardial tissue and does not form the normal muscular coat of the oesophagus.
notes.C: The upper oesophagus requires a developed muscular coat to propel swallowed material, rather than lacking muscle entirely.
notes.E: Smooth muscle predominates in the lower oesophageal third rather than the proximal striated muscular region.

questions.stem: Oesophageal atresia and stenosis are thought to result from

options.label: B
options.text: failure of the vitelline duct to close

options.label: E
options.text: failure of recanalisation of the lumen

questions.why: The oesophageal lumen is temporarily occluded by epithelium; failure to recanalise gives stenosis or atresia.

questions.stem: The stomach first appears during week 4 as a fusiform dilatation of the
questions.why: The stomach first appears as a fusiform expansion of the embryonic foregut during the fourth week. Differential growth and subsequent rotation establish its curvatures, adult orientation and characteristic relationships with adjacent peritoneal structures.

notes.B: The midgut forms much of the small intestine and proximal colon rather than the initial gastric primordium.
notes.C: The hindgut contributes distal colonic and rectal structures rather than the developing stomach.
notes.D: The yolk sac contributes incorporated gut endoderm, but the specific gastric dilatation occurs within the foregut.
notes.E: The allantois extends from the caudal embryonic region and does not form the foregut gastric expansion.

questions.stem: The stomach rotates 90 degrees clockwise about its longitudinal axis, which explains why the

options.label: B
options.text: left vagus supplies the anterior wall

options.label: C
options.text: right vagus supplies the anterior wall

options.label: D
options.text: left vagus supplies the lesser curvature

questions.why: Viewed from the cranial end, the stomach rotates approximately ninety degrees clockwise around its longitudinal axis. Its original left surface becomes anterior, carrying the left vagal supply into the predominantly anterior vagal trunk.

notes.A: Cardia displacement is not the characteristic consequence defining the vagal relationship after longitudinal gastric rotation.
notes.C: The original right gastric surface becomes posterior, carrying right vagal fibres into the predominantly posterior vagal trunk.
notes.D: Left vagal fibres principally follow the original left gastric surface, rather than exclusively supplying the lesser curvature.
notes.E: The pylorus shifts rightward and superiorly during gastric reorientation, rather than moving towards the left.

questions.stem: The greater curvature of the stomach forms because its dorsal border

options.label: B
options.text: is tethered by the lesser omentum

options.label: C
options.text: grows faster than the ventral border

questions.why: The dorsal gastric wall grows more rapidly than the ventral wall, producing the larger convex greater curvature. The relatively shorter ventral border forms the lesser curvature as the stomach enlarges and rotates.

notes.A: The pancreas develops in close dorsal gastric relationships but does not create the greater curvature through gastric fusion.
notes.B: The lesser omentum attaches along the lesser curvature and does not principally generate dorsal gastric differential growth.
notes.D: Rotation changes gastric orientation, whereas unequal dorsal and ventral wall growth establishes the curvature size difference.
notes.E: Splenic development within the dorsal mesogastrium accompanies gastric rearrangement but does not mechanically generate the greater curvature.

questions.stem: The omental bursa (lesser sac) forms behind the stomach as a consequence of
questions.why: Gastric rotation displaces the dorsal mesogastrium and creates a recess behind the developing stomach. This recess expands as the omental bursa, or lesser sac, communicating with the greater peritoneal sac through the epiploic foramen.

notes.A: Diaphragmatic descent alters thoracoabdominal relationships but is not the principal mechanism creating the retrogastric peritoneal recess.
notes.B: Midgut rotation positions intestinal loops around the superior mesenteric artery rather than creating the lesser sac behind the stomach.
