notes.C: The spleen develops within dorsal mesogastrium but its formation is not the primary mechanism of omental bursa development.
notes.E: Liver growth modifies ventral mesentery derivatives, whereas gastric rotation displaces dorsal mesogastrium to form the lesser sac.

questions.stem: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents with
questions.why: Hypertrophy of pyloric circular smooth muscle narrows the gastric outlet and impedes passage into the duodenum. Infants classically develop progressive forceful non-bilious projectile vomiting because obstruction lies proximal to biliary entry.

notes.A: Bile-stained vomiting suggests obstruction distal to biliary entry, whereas pyloric narrowing occurs proximal to this point.
notes.B: Failure to pass meconium suggests distal intestinal obstruction rather than the typical presentation of gastric outlet obstruction.
notes.C: Painless rectal bleeding may occur with Meckel's diverticulum rather than being characteristic of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
notes.D: Abdominal wall defects involve external herniation of viscera rather than narrowing of the pyloric gastric outlet.

questions.stem: Growth of the liver into the ventral mesentery divides it into the falciform ligament and the
questions.why: The hepatic diverticulum expands into the ventral foregut mesentery, separating it into a portion between liver and stomach or proximal duodenum and another between liver and anterior body wall. These become lesser omentum and falciform ligament respectively.

notes.B: The greater omentum develops from elongated dorsal mesogastrium, rather than the divided ventral foregut mesentery.
notes.C: Gastrosplenic ligament develops from dorsal mesogastrium between stomach and spleen, rather than the liver-associated ventral mesentery.
notes.D: Lienorenal ligament develops from dorsal mesogastrium between spleen and posterior abdominal wall, not the ventral mesentery.
notes.E: Coronary ligaments reflect hepatic peritoneal attachments, but lesser omentum is the specified other principal ventral mesentery derivative.

questions.stem: The spleen develops within the
questions.why: The spleen develops from mesenchymal condensations within the dorsal mesogastrium rather than from gut endoderm. Gastric rotation subsequently moves it towards the left and establishes its gastrosplenic and lienorenal ligament relationships.

notes.A: The urorectal septum partitions the cloaca and does not give rise to the splenic mesenchymal primordium.
notes.C: Ventral mesogastrium contributes falciform ligament and lesser omentum, whereas splenic mesenchyme develops dorsally.
notes.D: Septum transversum receives the hepatic diverticulum rather than containing the conventional splenic primordium.
notes.E: Falciform ligament develops from ventral mesentery and does not enclose the developing splenic mesenchymal condensation.

questions.stem: The ligament connecting the spleen to the posterior body wall at the kidney is the
questions.why: The lienorenal or splenorenal ligament is a dorsal mesogastrium derivative connecting the splenic hilum to the posterior abdominal wall near the left kidney. It contains splenic vessels and is related to the pancreatic tail.

notes.A: The lesser omentum connects liver to stomach and proximal duodenum rather than spleen to posterior abdominal wall.
notes.B: Hepatoduodenal ligament is the free edge of lesser omentum containing the portal triad, not the splenic attachment.
notes.D: Gastrosplenic ligament connects the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach, rather than the kidney region.
notes.E: Falciform ligament connects liver to anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, rather than attaching the spleen posteriorly.

questions.stem: The free margin of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) contains the
questions.why: The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the free right margin of the lesser omentum and carries the portal vein, proper hepatic artery and bile duct. These structures constitute the portal triad at this location.

notes.A: Superior mesenteric vessels pass within the intestinal mesentery and are not the portal triad within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
notes.B: The thoracic duct carries lymph through the posterior mediastinum rather than traversing the free lesser omental margin.
notes.C: Cisterna chyli is a lymphatic collecting structure near the posterior abdominal wall rather than the portal triad.
notes.E: Splenic vessels course towards the spleen in dorsal peritoneal relationships, not within the free hepatoduodenal margin.

questions.stem: The liver develops as the hepatic bud, an outgrowth of the foregut that grows into the
questions.why: The hepatic diverticulum arises from ventral distal foregut endoderm and grows into the septum transversum mesenchyme. Reciprocal interactions promote hepatic epithelial differentiation, while adjacent mesenchyme contributes stromal and vascular support to the developing liver.

notes.A: The dorsal mesogastrium contains the developing spleen and does not receive the hepatic diverticulum as its principal site.
notes.B: Pleuroperitoneal membranes contribute to diaphragm development rather than serving as the initial hepatic growth substrate.
notes.C: The urorectal septum develops near the cloaca, well caudal to the embryonic hepatic diverticulum.
notes.D: The yolk sac contributes early blood and gut development but is not the mesenchymal site invaded by the hepatic bud.

questions.stem: The hepatocytes of the liver are derived from
questions.why: Hepatocytes differentiate from endodermal cells of the hepatic diverticulum arising in the ventral foregut. Mesenchymal and vascular populations contribute supporting tissue and sinusoidal organisation rather than forming the principal hepatic epithelial lineage.

notes.B: Septum transversum mesenchyme provides inductive and stromal contributions, rather than directly generating most liver hepatocytes.
notes.C: Vitelline venous remodelling contributes hepatic sinusoids and portal venous structures rather than the endoderm-derived hepatocyte population.
notes.D: Neural crest contributes selected neural and connective tissues but is not the developmental source of hepatocytes.
notes.E: Splanchnic mesoderm contributes supporting mesenchymal tissues, whereas hepatocytes originate from the hepatic endodermal diverticulum.

questions.stem: The gallbladder and cystic duct develop from the
questions.why: The caudal portion of the hepatic diverticulum develops as the cystic bud, forming the gallbladder and cystic duct. The larger cranial hepatic component contributes liver epithelial tissue and associated biliary structures.

notes.A: Dorsal mesogastrium contributes splenic and other dorsal peritoneal structures rather than forming gallbladder epithelium.
notes.C: The dorsal pancreatic bud forms substantial pancreatic tissue rather than the gallbladder and its drainage duct.
notes.D: The hepatic duct system is closely related to the cystic bud but is not the specific gallbladder primordium.
notes.E: The ventral pancreatic bud produces pancreatic tissue, including the uncinate process, rather than the gallbladder.

questions.stem: The uncinate process and lower part of the head of the pancreas develop from the
questions.why: The ventral pancreatic bud rotates posteriorly with the duodenum and fuses with the dorsal pancreatic bud. It contributes the uncinate process and inferior pancreatic head, while the dorsal bud forms most remaining pancreatic tissue.

notes.A: The cystic bud forms gallbladder and cystic duct rather than the lower pancreatic head and uncinate process.
notes.B: The spleen develops from mesenchyme within dorsal mesogastrium and does not supply pancreatic epithelial tissue.
notes.D: The dorsal pancreatic bud contributes body, tail and much of the head rather than the characteristic uncinate process.
notes.E: The hepatic bud forms liver and associated biliary derivatives, rather than the ventral pancreatic component.

questions.stem: The superior mesenteric artery comes to lie anterior to the uncinate process because of
questions.why: Rotation and growth of the duodenum carry the ventral pancreatic bud posteriorly towards the dorsal bud. The resulting uncinate process extends behind the superior mesenteric vessels, accounting for their anterior relationship to it.

notes.A: Duodenal rearrangement accompanies the process, but ventral pancreatic bud migration establishes the specific uncinate vascular relationship.
notes.B: Splenic growth occurs within dorsal mesogastrium and does not directly determine the uncinate process position behind mesenteric vessels.
notes.C: Mesenteric fusion contributes secondary retroperitoneal relationships rather than specifically establishing the ventral bud-derived uncinate process.
notes.E: Gastric rotation affects nearby organ relationships, but the relevant immediate developmental mechanism is ventral pancreatic bud migration.

questions.stem: The midgut extends from the opening of the bile duct to the
questions.why: The embryonic midgut begins in the duodenum distal to the bile duct opening and extends to approximately the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. This region retains its characteristic superior mesenteric arterial supply.

notes.A: The splenic flexure is closer to the distal transverse colon and does not precisely identify the embryonic midgut endpoint.
notes.B: The rectosigmoid junction lies within hindgut-derived intestine, considerably distal to the midgut arterial territory.
notes.C: The duodenojejunal junction lies within the early midgut pathway rather than marking its distal endpoint.
notes.D: The ileocaecal valve lies within midgut derivatives; the midgut also supplies the ascending and proximal transverse colon.

questions.stem: Physiological herniation of the midgut into the umbilical cord occurs during week
questions.why: Rapid midgut elongation and limited abdominal capacity cause physiological umbilical herniation around the sixth embryonic week. The intestinal loops subsequently rotate and normally return to the expanding abdominal cavity around the tenth week.

notes.B: The fourth week establishes the primitive gut and embryonic folding before the normal period of physiological midgut herniation.
notes.C: The tenth week is conventionally associated with intestinal return to the abdomen, rather than the onset of herniation.
notes.D: By the twelfth week the intestinal loops normally occupy the abdominal cavity rather than beginning physiological herniation.
notes.E: The sixteenth week occurs well after normal midgut herniation, rotation and return during the embryonic period.

questions.stem: During its development the midgut loop rotates a total of
questions.why: The midgut loop normally rotates approximately 270 degrees counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery when viewed anteriorly. An initial ninety-degree rotation accompanies herniation, followed by further rotation as the bowel returns.

notes.A: Ninety degrees describes the initial rotation during physiological herniation, not the total developmental rotation.
notes.C: Clockwise rotation is opposite the conventional normal direction when the developing intestinal loop is viewed anteriorly.
notes.D: One hundred and eighty degrees represents the later component of rotation but omits the earlier ninety-degree movement.
notes.E: A full 360-degree rotation exceeds the conventional total of 270 degrees around the superior mesenteric arterial axis.

questions.stem: The caecum and appendix develop from the

options.label: E
options.text: cranial limb of the midgut loop

questions.why: The caecal diverticulum appears as a swelling of the caudal limb of the primary midgut loop. Its proximal region expands to form the caecum, while its narrower distal portion forms the vermiform appendix.

notes.A: The hindgut forms distal colon and rectal structures, whereas caecum and appendix are midgut derivatives.
notes.B: The hepatic bud contributes liver and biliary structures rather than the diverticulum forming caecum and appendix.
notes.D: The vitelline duct connects midgut to yolk sac and may persist as Meckel's diverticulum rather than the appendix.
notes.E: The cranial limb principally develops small intestinal loops, whereas caecal diverticulum arises from the caudal limb.

questions.stem: Failure of the herniated midgut loop to return to the abdomen, leaving viscera in a sac covered by amnion, is
questions.why: Omphalocoele involves congenital herniation of abdominal viscera through the umbilical ring into a membrane-covered sac. Persistence of herniated intestinal contents or abnormal ventral wall development prevents their normal enclosure within the abdomen.

notes.A: Meckel's diverticulum is a persistent vitelline duct remnant within the ileum, rather than external membrane-covered visceral herniation.
notes.B: An ordinary umbilical hernia is covered by skin and differs from an omphalocoele sac containing exposed fetal membranes.
notes.C: Volvulus involves twisting of bowel around its mesenteric axis rather than failure of abdominal enclosure.
notes.E: Gastroschisis involves a usually paraumbilical wall defect with bowel lacking the protective covering characteristic of omphalocoele.

questions.stem: Gastroschisis differs from omphalocoele in that the herniated bowel

options.label: E
options.text: is not covered by a membrane

questions.why: Gastroschisis is a congenital full-thickness abdominal wall defect, usually to the right of the umbilicus, through which bowel protrudes without a covering sac. Omphalocoele instead occurs through the umbilical ring with membrane-covered contents.

notes.A: Bowel within a membrane-covered umbilical cord sac is characteristic of omphalocoele rather than typical gastroschisis.
notes.B: Gastroschisis bowel lacks a protective amniotic covering, unlike the membrane-covered contents of omphalocoele.
notes.C: Gastroschisis commonly involves small bowel and can involve other organs, rather than being limited to large bowel.
notes.D: The defect is usually paraumbilical rather than situated directly in the umbilical midline as in omphalocoele.

questions.stem: Meckel's diverticulum is a persistent remnant of the
questions.why: Meckel's diverticulum results from persistence of the intestinal end of the vitelline or omphalomesenteric duct. It forms a true diverticulum of the antimesenteric ileum and may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue.

notes.B: The urachus is associated with allantoic and bladder development rather than the persistent intestinal yolk sac connection.
notes.C: The cystic duct connects gallbladder with the biliary tree and does not form the ileal diverticulum.
notes.D: The thyroglossal duct connects the developing thyroid to its lingual origin and may produce cervical cysts.
notes.E: The allantois contributes to urachal development, not the vitelline duct remnant that forms Meckel's diverticulum.

questions.stem: The hindgut gives rise to the descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and the

options.label: B
options.text: upper two-thirds of the anal canal

options.label: C
options.text: lower third of the anal canal

questions.why: Hindgut endoderm contributes the distal transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum and upper anal canal above the pectinate line. The lower anal canal instead develops from the ectodermal proctodeum.

notes.A: The proximal transverse colon derives primarily from midgut, retaining the characteristic superior mesenteric arterial supply.
notes.C: The lower third of the anal canal derives from ectodermal proctodeum rather than hindgut endoderm.
notes.D: The anal canal has dual embryological origins, so the entire canal cannot be assigned to hindgut endoderm.
notes.E: Caecum and appendix derive from the caecal diverticulum of the midgut rather than hindgut.

questions.stem: The cloaca is partitioned into a urogenital sinus and a rectoanal canal by the
questions.why: The developing urorectal septum partitions the cloacal region into a ventral urogenital sinus and dorsal anorectal canal. Its remodelling contributes to separation of urinary and digestive outlets and formation of the perineal region.

notes.A: The allantois extends from the ventral cloacal region but is not the mesenchymal partition separating the two pathways.
notes.B: The vitelline duct connects the midgut with the yolk sac and does not divide the caudal cloaca.
notes.D: The urogenital membrane covers the future ventral outlet after partitioning, rather than generating the separating septum.
notes.E: The perineal body develops at the region of separation but does not alone partition the original cloacal cavity.

questions.stem: The lower one-third of the anal canal (below the pectinate line) is derived from
questions.why: The lower anal canal develops from the proctodeum, an ectodermal invagination that meets the endoderm-derived hindgut. Their developmental junction at the pectinate line explains differences in epithelium, vascular drainage and sensory innervation.

notes.A: Midgut endoderm contributes proximal intestinal regions, not the ectoderm-derived lower anal canal below the pectinate line.
notes.B: Splanchnic mesoderm contributes gut supporting tissues and muscle rather than the proctodeal epithelial lining.
notes.C: Neural crest contributes enteric ganglia, rather than the epithelial tissue forming the lower anal canal.
notes.E: Hindgut endoderm contributes the upper anal canal above the pectinate line, not its lower ectodermal portion.

questions.stem: Above the pectinate line the anal canal is supplied by the superior rectal artery, a branch of the
questions.why: The upper anal canal retains hindgut-related arterial supply through the superior rectal artery, the terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery. Anastomoses with middle and inferior rectal branches connect adjacent vascular territories.

notes.A: The internal iliac artery commonly gives rise to middle rectal supply rather than the superior rectal artery.
notes.B: The internal pudendal artery gives rise to inferior rectal branches supplying the lower anal canal and surrounding tissues.
notes.C: The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut derivatives rather than the superior rectal continuation of hindgut arterial supply.
notes.D: The median sacral artery courses along the sacrum and is not the parent vessel of the superior rectal artery.

questions.stem: Below the pectinate line the anal canal is sensitive to pain because it is supplied by the
questions.why: Below the pectinate line, the anal canal has somatic sensory innervation through inferior rectal branches of the pudendal nerve. This enables relatively precise perception of pain, touch and temperature compared with visceral innervation above.

notes.B: The inferior hypogastric plexus carries visceral autonomic and sensory fibres rather than the principal somatic pain supply below the line.
notes.C: Pelvic splanchnic nerves provide parasympathetic and visceral pathways rather than the characteristic lower anal canal somatic sensation.
notes.D: Superior rectal sensory pathways principally accompany visceral structures above the pectinate line rather than supplying lower somatic pain.
notes.E: The vagus supplies parasympathetic pathways to more proximal digestive regions and does not provide lower anal canal somatic sensation.

questions.stem: Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) results from failure of migration of
questions.why: Neural-crest-derived parasympathetic ganglion cells fail to populate the myenteric plexus of the distal colon, which cannot relax.

questions.stem: Imperforate anus and rectal fistulas arise mainly from abnormal development of the
questions.why: Anorectal malformations are associated with abnormal development and remodelling of the cloacal region, including the urorectal septum. Impaired separation of digestive and urogenital pathways may produce abnormal openings, atresia or fistulas.

notes.A: The perineal body contributes to separation of the outlets but does not alone explain the range of anorectal malformations.
notes.B: Proctodeal abnormalities may affect distal anal formation, but fistulas also involve abnormal partitioning of the cloacal region.
notes.D: Vitelline duct remnants produce ileal or umbilical abnormalities rather than the characteristic anorectal and urinary tract fistulas.
notes.E: The allantois contributes to urachal development, rather than being the principal partition between anorectal and urogenital compartments.

questions.stem: The neonate's first stool, a sticky greenish-black material, is called
questions.why: Meconium is the newborn's initial intestinal content, typically thick and greenish-black because it contains bile pigments, shed epithelial cells and swallowed substances. Passage after birth reflects establishment of intestinal transit.

notes.A: Lanugo is fine fetal hair covering the skin, rather than the material passed as the first stool.
notes.B: Vernix caseosa is the protective lipid-rich coating on fetal skin, not the initial intestinal contents.
notes.C: Chyme describes partially digested material leaving the stomach rather than the accumulated first neonatal stool.
notes.E: Colostrum is the early mammary secretion rich in protective factors, rather than the first material passed from the intestine.

questions.stem: The kidneys and ureters develop from which germ layer derivative?
questions.why: The urinary system's kidneys and ureters arise from intermediate mesoderm, which forms the nephrogenic cord and its associated epithelial systems. The definitive kidney develops through interaction between metanephric mesenchyme and ureteric bud.

notes.B: Splanchnic mesoderm contributes visceral connective tissue and smooth muscle, rather than the primary nephrogenic cord.
notes.C: Surface ectoderm forms external epithelial and selected sensory structures rather than the renal and ureteric primordia.
notes.D: Endoderm contributes much of the lower urinary tract lining, but kidneys and ureters originate from intermediate mesoderm.
notes.E: Neural crest supplies peripheral neural and other derivatives, rather than the principal epithelial and mesenchymal renal primordia.

questions.stem: The three successive kidney systems that develop in the embryo are the pronephros, mesonephros and
questions.why: Three successive renal systems form from intermediate mesoderm: pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros. The first regresses early, the second functions temporarily, and the metanephros develops into the permanent kidney.

notes.A: The nephrogenic cord is the intermediate mesodermal region producing successive renal systems rather than the third kidney system.
notes.C: The mesonephric duct drains the transient mesonephros and produces the ureteric bud, but is not itself the definitive kidney.
notes.D: Allantois contributes to urachal development and does not represent a successive embryonic renal system.
notes.E: The ureteric or metanephric diverticulum forms the collecting system but is only one component of the metanephros.

questions.stem: The pronephros appears in the cervical region during week 4 and is
questions.why: The human pronephros appears transiently in the cervical intermediate mesoderm early in the fourth week and rapidly regresses. It does not function as a mature excretory kidney, unlike the subsequent metanephros.

notes.A: The pronephros develops from intermediate mesoderm, rather than from the endodermal epithelium of the embryonic gut.
notes.B: The urinary bladder develops mainly from the vesical urogenital sinus rather than the transient cervical pronephros.
notes.D: The metanephros forms the permanent kidney, whereas the pronephros regresses early during human embryonic development.
notes.E: The ureter arises from the ureteric bud of the mesonephric duct rather than directly from pronephric tubules.

questions.stem: The duct that drains the mesonephros is the
questions.why: The mesonephric or Wolffian duct receives drainage from the developing mesonephric tubules and opens into the cloacal region. It later gives rise to the ureteric bud and persists in males as genital ducts.

notes.A: The ureteric bud branches from the mesonephric duct and develops the collecting system of the definitive kidney.
notes.B: The metanephric collecting pathway develops from the ureteric bud, rather than draining the earlier mesonephric tubules.
notes.C: The vitelline duct connects the embryonic midgut to the yolk sac and is unrelated to mesonephric drainage.
notes.E: The paramesonephric duct forms much of the female reproductive tract rather than draining the transient mesonephric kidney.

questions.stem: In the male, a few mesonephric tubules persist as the functional
questions.why: Some mesonephric tubules near the developing testis persist and connect the rete testis to the epididymal duct. They form efferent ductules, while the mesonephric duct itself forms much of the male genital drainage system.

notes.A: Seminiferous tubules develop from testicular sex cords and do not arise from persistent mesonephric tubules.
notes.B: Renal collecting ducts derive from ureteric bud branches rather than the mesonephric tubules retained beside the testis.
notes.C: The rete testis develops from testicular cord-associated structures rather than being the mesonephric tubule derivative specified.
notes.D: The appendix of the epididymis is a vestigial duct-related remnant, rather than the functional efferent ductules.

questions.stem: Remnants of the mesonephric tubules in the female form the vestigial epoophoron and
questions.why: In females, most mesonephric tubules regress, but cranial and caudal tubular remnants may persist within the broad ligament as the epoophoron and paroophoron. These vestiges differ from remnants of the mesonephric duct itself.

notes.B: Gartner cysts arise from persistent mesonephric duct tissue rather than the characteristic paired groups of tubular remnants.
notes.C: Ovarian follicles form from oocytes and surrounding somatic supporting cells, not residual mesonephric tubules.
notes.D: The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold that may contain these remnants rather than itself deriving from the tubules.
notes.E: The round ligament of the uterus derives from the gubernaculum rather than persistent female mesonephric tubules.

questions.stem: The definitive metanephros (permanent kidney) is formed by the metanephric blastema and the
questions.why: The metanephros develops through reciprocal inductive signalling between metanephric mesenchyme and the branching ureteric bud. The mesenchyme generates nephron epithelial structures, while the bud contributes the collecting system and ureter.

notes.A: The allantois contributes to urachal development rather than interacting with metanephric mesenchyme to form the permanent kidney.
notes.C: Mesonephric tubules form a transient kidney and selected genital derivatives rather than the definitive collecting tree.
notes.D: The pronephric duct belongs to earlier renal development, while the ureteric bud directly interacts with metanephric mesenchyme.
notes.E: The paramesonephric duct contributes female genital tract development rather than the epithelial collecting system of the metanephros.

questions.stem: The ureteric bud gives rise to the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and the
questions.why: The ureteric bud branches repeatedly within metanephric mesenchyme, generating the collecting duct system, calyces and renal pelvis. Its original stalk forms the ureter, connecting the definitive kidney to the developing bladder.

notes.A: Bowman's capsule develops from metanephric nephron progenitors rather than branching epithelium of the ureteric bud.
notes.B: Proximal tubules derive from metanephric mesenchyme through nephron epithelialisation rather than the collecting duct lineage.
notes.D: Nephrons arise principally from metanephric mesenchyme, with their distal ends joining the ureteric bud-derived collecting ducts.
notes.E: Glomerular epithelial podocytes derive from nephron progenitors, while vascular endothelial cells enter the developing glomerular tuft.

questions.stem: The nephrons (from glomerulus to distal convoluted tubule) are derived from the
questions.why: Metanephric mesenchyme forms epithelial renal vesicles that differentiate into nephron segments, including Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal tubule. Their distal connections join the separate ureteric bud-derived collecting system.

notes.A: The mesonephric duct gives rise to the ureteric bud but does not directly generate the definitive nephron epithelium.
notes.B: The allantois is associated with the urachus and bladder apex, rather than development of renal nephron segments.
notes.C: The urogenital sinus contributes to bladder and urethral development, not the metanephric nephron epithelial lineage.
notes.E: The ureteric bud gives rise to collecting ducts and drainage pathways rather than the nephron's tubular components.

questions.stem: Failure of a metanephric vesicle to connect with the collecting system may produce a
questions.why: Failure of developing nephron structures to connect appropriately with collecting ducts is a classical proposed mechanism of congenital renal cyst formation. Abnormal tubular development and drainage can cause cystic dilatation, although congenital cystic diseases have diverse mechanisms.

notes.A: A horseshoe kidney results from fusion of renal primordia and abnormal ascent, rather than an isolated nephron connection defect.
notes.B: A pelvic kidney results from abnormal renal ascent, rather than failure of renal vesicles to join collecting ducts.
notes.C: A bifid ureter develops from early branching or duplication of the ureteric bud rather than nephron connection failure.
notes.D: Wilms tumour arises from abnormal renal developmental precursors and is not simply a cyst caused by failed tubular connection.

questions.stem: The permanent kidney first forms in the pelvis and then ascends to lie opposite the
questions.why: The kidney ascends from the pelvis to the upper lumbar region, reaching about L2.

questions.stem: During ascent the kidney is supplied in turn by progressively higher branches of the aorta; a persisting lower vessel is an
questions.why: As kidneys move from their initial pelvic position, their arterial supply changes through successive branches from progressively higher vessels. Persistence of an earlier arterial connection produces an accessory renal artery supplying part of the kidney.

notes.A: Suprarenal arteries principally supply adrenal tissue rather than representing persistent embryonic renal blood supply pathways.
notes.C: Arcuate arteries course along the corticomedullary boundary within the kidney rather than representing persistent external renal vessels.
notes.D: Interlobar arteries run between renal pyramids and are not the extra arterial connections retained during kidney ascent.
notes.E: Segmental arteries supply renal vascular territories after branching, rather than necessarily representing persistent earlier aortic connections.

questions.stem: As it ascends, the kidney rotates about its longitudinal axis so that the hilum comes to face
questions.why: During renal ascent, the developing kidneys reorient so that their initially anterior hila come to face medially. This rotation establishes the adult arrangement of renal vessels and pelvis at the medial renal border.

notes.A: A posterior hilum represents abnormal rotation rather than the usual medial orientation of the adult renal hilum.
notes.B: The inferior pole becomes an anatomical kidney landmark but is not the normal orientation of the renal hilum.
notes.D: A lateral-facing hilum may reflect abnormal renal rotation and differs from the typical medial adult arrangement.
notes.E: The early renal hilum faces anteriorly, but normally becomes directed medially during development and relative ascent.

questions.stem: A kidney that fails to ascend and remains in the pelvis is a
questions.why: A pelvic kidney remains in its initial lower position because normal relative renal ascent does not occur. It may retain unusual arterial supply from nearby vessels and can have altered orientation or drainage.

notes.A: Cross-fused renal ectopia involves migration across the midline and fusion with the opposite kidney, not simple failed ascent.
notes.B: A duplex kidney has duplicated collecting structures rather than necessarily remaining in the pelvis during development.
notes.C: A supernumerary kidney is an additional renal organ, rather than one of the ordinary kidneys failing to ascend.
notes.E: A horseshoe kidney involves fusion of renal poles, often limiting ascent, but pelvic ectopia does not require fusion.

questions.stem: A horseshoe kidney becomes trapped during ascent at the
questions.why: In a horseshoe kidney, fusion of the lower renal poles creates an isthmus that can limit upward movement. Classically, the inferior mesenteric artery obstructs further ascent, leaving the kidney lower than usual.

notes.A: The coeliac trunk arises much higher in the abdomen and is not the classical vessel limiting horseshoe kidney ascent.
notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery lies above the inferior mesenteric artery and is not the usual teaching obstruction.
notes.C: Renal arteries develop changing supply relationships during ascent rather than forming the characteristic inferior mesenteric arterial barrier.
notes.D: The aortic bifurcation lies below the classical arterial level associated with arrest of horseshoe kidney ascent.

questions.stem: Double or bifid ureters arise from an abnormality of the
questions.why: Premature division of a ureteric bud can produce a bifid collecting system, while formation of two buds may produce complete ureteric duplication. The resulting anatomy depends on the timing and extent of epithelial branching.

notes.B: Metanephric mesenchyme generates nephron structures rather than the primary ureteric epithelial stalk and its branching pattern.
notes.C: Mesonephric tubules contribute transient renal and selected genital structures, rather than producing duplicated definitive ureters directly.
notes.D: The urogenital sinus forms much of the bladder and urethra rather than the original branching renal collecting system.
notes.E: Allantoic remnants may produce urachal abnormalities, rather than duplication of the ureters arising from ureteric buds.

questions.stem: The urinary bladder develops mainly from the
questions.why: The vesical portion of the endoderm-lined urogenital sinus expands to form most of the urinary bladder. Its surrounding mesenchyme supplies smooth muscle and connective tissue, while the allantoic connection normally becomes the urachus.

notes.A: Hindgut contributes the anorectal pathway after cloacal partitioning, rather than most of the urinary bladder.
notes.C: The allantois connects to the developing bladder apex but does not form the entire bladder cavity.
notes.D: Mesonephric duct incorporation contributes to trigonal development, but most bladder tissue derives from the urogenital sinus.
notes.E: Metanephric blastema generates renal nephron structures rather than the vesical portion of the urogenital sinus.

questions.stem: The epithelium lining the urinary bladder is derived from
questions.why: Most bladder urothelium develops from endoderm of the vesical urogenital sinus. Although the trigonal region is associated with incorporated mesonephric ducts, its epithelial surface is subsequently covered by endoderm-derived urothelium.

notes.A: Surface ectoderm contributes selected distal epithelial structures rather than the main lining of the bladder.
notes.B: Neural crest contributes autonomic and sensory neural structures, not the endodermal bladder epithelial population.
notes.D: Intermediate mesoderm contributes renal and mesonephric structures but does not form most mature bladder urothelium.
notes.E: Splanchnic mesoderm contributes bladder smooth muscle and connective tissue rather than its endodermal epithelial lining.

questions.stem: The trigone of the bladder is formed by incorporation of the
questions.why: In the classical developmental description, incorporation of the caudal mesonephric ducts into the posterior bladder wall contributes to formation of the trigone. Its surface epithelium is subsequently replaced by endoderm-derived urothelium.

notes.A: Paramesonephric ducts form female genital structures and are not the ducts incorporated into the developing bladder trigone.
notes.B: The allantois connects the bladder apex to the umbilical region rather than forming the posterior trigonal area.
notes.C: The urachus is the remnant of the allantoic bladder connection, not the developmental source of the trigone.
notes.E: Ureteric buds give rise to the ureters and collecting systems, while incorporation involves their parent mesonephric duct region.

questions.stem: After birth the obliterated allantois (urachus) persists as the
questions.why: The allantoic connection between the bladder apex and umbilicus normally becomes obliterated as the urachus. Its fibrous adult remnant is the median umbilical ligament, located in the midline beneath the anterior abdominal wall.

notes.A: Medial umbilical ligaments are paired remnants of distal umbilical arteries rather than the single midline urachal remnant.
notes.B: Lateral umbilical folds overlie inferior epigastric vessels and do not represent obliterated allantoic tissue.
notes.C: The round ligament of the liver derives from the left umbilical vein, rather than the urachus.
notes.D: Falciform ligament attaches liver to the anterior abdominal wall and is not the fibrous remnant of the allantois.

questions.stem: Persistence of the urachal lumen giving urine discharge at the umbilicus is a
questions.why: A patent urachus persists as an open channel connecting the urinary bladder apex to the umbilicus. Urine can pass through this persistent embryonic connection and appear as drainage at the umbilicus.

notes.B: A urachal cyst contains a persistent central lumen with closed ends rather than a completely open bladder-to-umbilicus tract.
notes.C: A urachal sinus opens at the umbilicus but does not normally retain a complete connection to the bladder.
notes.D: A urachal diverticulum communicates with the bladder but does not extend as a patent channel to the umbilicus.
notes.E: Meckel's diverticulum derives from the vitelline duct and communicates with ileum rather than the urinary bladder.

questions.stem: Exstrophy of the bladder, in which the bladder opens onto the lower abdominal wall, is due to failure of
questions.why: Bladder exstrophy is a complex ventral midline developmental defect exposing bladder mucosa on the lower abdominal wall. The classical explanation involves deficient mesenchymal reinforcement of the cloacal membrane and premature disruption of this region.

notes.A: Urorectal septal abnormalities primarily affect separation of digestive and urogenital outlets, rather than the specific ventral exstrophy defect.
notes.C: Failure of urachal obliteration produces urine drainage at the umbilicus rather than exposing the bladder mucosa.
notes.D: Abnormal ureteric bud branching produces collecting system abnormalities rather than failure of the lower abdominal wall.
notes.E: Failed renal ascent causes ectopic kidney position and does not directly produce the ventral bladder wall defect.

questions.stem: The genetic (chromosomal) sex of the embryo is determined
questions.why: The usual chromosomal sex complement is established at fertilisation when an X-bearing oocyte combines with an X-bearing or Y-bearing sperm. Subsequent gene expression influences gonadal differentiation and development of reproductive anatomy.

notes.B: The seventh week is associated with early gonadal differentiation rather than initial determination of the zygote's chromosome complement.
notes.C: The twelfth week involves further differentiation of external genital structures, not establishment of chromosomal sex.
notes.D: Implantation occurs after fertilisation, when the conceptus already possesses its original sex chromosome complement.
notes.E: Gastrulation establishes embryonic germ layers after chromosomal sex has already been determined at fertilisation.

questions.stem: The gene on the Y chromosome that triggers testis formation is
questions.why: SRY, located on the Y chromosome, initiates the typical testis-determining pathway by promoting SOX9 expression in supporting cell precursors. This drives Sertoli cell differentiation and subsequent organisation of the fetal testis.

notes.A: SF1 participates in gonadal and adrenal development but is not the Y-linked testis-determining trigger specified here.
notes.C: SOX9 is a critical downstream testicular differentiation regulator, but it is not the Y-chromosomal gene itself.
notes.D: WNT4 supports ovarian developmental signalling and is not the usual Y-linked initiator of testis formation.
notes.E: DAX1 participates in dosage-sensitive gonadal regulation rather than functioning as the principal Y-chromosomal testis determinant.

questions.stem: Until about week 7 the gonads are described as
questions.why: The early gonadal ridge is initially bipotential and lacks the definitive morphology of either testis or ovary. Around the seventh week, testis-specific differentiation becomes apparent in typical XY development, while ovarian differentiation becomes evident later.

notes.A: Gonadal primordia are present before sexual differentiation, rather than being absent until the seventh embryonic week.
notes.B: Early gonads retain developmental potential for both pathways and are not yet fully differentiated into mature reproductive organs.
notes.D: Typical male gonadal morphology emerges after activation of testis-determining pathways, rather than being evident throughout the indifferent stage.
notes.E: Typical ovarian morphology develops after the initial bipotential period rather than being identifiable from the earliest gonadal ridge.

questions.stem: Primordial germ cells first arise in the
questions.why: PGCs differentiate in the yolk-sac endoderm near the allantois and migrate to the gonadal ridge via the dorsal mesentery.

questions.stem: Primordial germ cells reach the gonadal ridge by migrating along the
questions.why: Primordial germ cells migrate from the yolk sac region into the developing hindgut and subsequently through its dorsal mesentery towards the gonadal ridges. Their arrival contributes to establishment of the developing germ-cell population.

notes.A: The ventral body wall is not the conventional migration route linking the hindgut region with the developing gonadal ridges.
notes.B: Neural crest migration produces distinct cell populations and does not provide the principal route of primordial germ cells.
notes.C: The mesonephric duct develops as a renal drainage pathway rather than the migratory path followed by germ cells.
notes.D: The allantoic region is near early germ-cell locations, but migration to gonadal ridges proceeds through the dorsal mesentery.

questions.stem: The gonadal (genital) ridge arises on the medial side of the
questions.why: The gonadal ridge forms through proliferation of coelomic epithelium and condensation of underlying mesenchyme along the medial aspect of the mesonephros. Migrating primordial germ cells subsequently colonise this developing gonadal primordium.

notes.B: The metanephros develops as the definitive kidney and is not the initial structure adjoining the gonadal ridge.
notes.C: The hindgut provides part of the germ-cell migration pathway rather than the immediate location of gonadal ridge formation.
notes.D: The neural tube forms the central nervous system and is not the adjacent renal structure defining the gonadal ridge.
notes.E: The dorsal aorta lies nearby but the ridge is classically identified along the medial surface of the mesonephros.

questions.stem: In the testis, the Sertoli cells are derived from the
questions.why: Somatic supporting cell precursors within the developing testicular sex cords differentiate into Sertoli cells under testis-determining signalling. They organise germ cells within cords and secrete anti-Müllerian hormone during fetal development.

notes.A: Tunica albuginea is a fibrous capsule developing around the testis, rather than the supporting cell lineage of sex cords.
notes.C: Primordial germ cells produce the spermatogenic lineage rather than the somatic Sertoli population supporting it.
notes.D: Interstitial mesenchyme contributes steroidogenic Leydig cells and other stromal components rather than the principal supporting sex cord cells.
notes.E: Mesonephric tubules form efferent ductules in males, rather than differentiating into the Sertoli cells of testicular cords.

questions.stem: Testosterone is first produced in the fetal testis by the
questions.why: Fetal Leydig cells differentiate within testicular interstitial tissue and synthesise testosterone in response to developmental endocrine signals. Testosterone promotes maintenance and differentiation of mesonephric ducts into the male internal genital tract.

notes.A: Rete testis cells form part of the sperm drainage pathway rather than the principal fetal steroidogenic population.
notes.B: Germ cells develop into gametes and do not provide the main fetal source of circulating testosterone.
notes.D: Sertoli cells principally provide developmental support and anti-Müllerian hormone, while Leydig cells produce testicular testosterone.
notes.E: Spermatogonia are germ-cell precursors and do not constitute the steroidogenic interstitial cell population.

questions.stem: Anti-Mullerian hormone (Mullerian inhibiting substance) is secreted by the
questions.why: In the differentiating fetal testis, Sertoli cells secrete anti-Müllerian hormone, inducing regression of paramesonephric ducts. Leydig-cell testosterone separately maintains mesonephric ducts, allowing typical male internal reproductive structures to develop.

notes.A: Ovarian granulosa cells can produce anti-Müllerian hormone later, but fetal testicular Sertoli cells provide the duct-regressing signal.
notes.B: Theca cells contribute ovarian steroid production and are not the primary source of fetal testicular anti-Müllerian hormone.
notes.C: Spermatogonia are germ-cell precursors rather than the somatic endocrine cells directing paramesonephric duct regression.
notes.E: Leydig cells secrete testosterone, which maintains mesonephric ducts rather than directly mediating Müllerian duct regression.

questions.stem: In the absence of SRY the gonad develops into an ovary, driven by
questions.why: Without SRY, WNT4 acting via DAX1 steers the bipotential gonad toward an ovary.

questions.stem: Oogonia enter meiosis and arrest as primary oocytes in
questions.why: During fetal ovarian development, oogonia proliferate and enter meiosis I to become primary oocytes. They arrest at the diplotene stage of prophase I and resume meiosis only when selected for later ovulation.

notes.B: Metaphase I follows resumption of meiosis and is not the prolonged arrest stage established during fetal ovarian development.
notes.C: Prophase II occurs after completion of meiosis I and does not describe the prolonged primary oocyte arrest.
notes.D: Metaphase II is the usual arrest of the ovulated secondary oocyte, not the primary oocyte during fetal development.
notes.E: Anaphase I involves homologous chromosome separation after meiotic resumption, rather than the stage at which primary oocytes remain arrested.

questions.stem: The number of primordial follicles is maximal at about
questions.why: About 7 million follicles exist at 5 months, falling to about 2 million at birth and 40,000 by puberty.

questions.stem: The male genital ducts (epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct) develop from the
questions.why: Under fetal testosterone influence, mesonephric or Wolffian ducts persist and differentiate into epididymal ducts, ductus deferens, seminal vesicle outgrowths and ejaculatory ducts. Their associated efferent ductules originate from selected mesonephric tubules.

notes.A: The metanephric collecting pathway forms ureters and renal collecting structures rather than the male genital drainage ducts.
notes.B: The genital tubercle contributes the external phallus rather than the internal male reproductive duct system.
notes.D: Paramesonephric ducts typically regress in male development under anti-Müllerian hormone influence rather than forming the listed genital ducts.
notes.E: The urogenital sinus contributes prostate and urethral structures rather than the principal mesonephric duct-derived male genital passages.

questions.stem: The uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina develop from the
questions.why: The paramesonephric or Müllerian ducts contribute the uterine tubes and, after caudal fusion, the uterus and upper vaginal region in classical embryology. The developing vaginal epithelium and lower tract also involve urogenital sinus contributions.

notes.A: The urogenital sinus contributes vaginal and lower urinary tract development, but does not form the uterine tubes and uterus.
notes.B: Metanephric blastema produces renal nephron structures rather than the epithelial reproductive tract derived from paired genital ducts.
notes.C: The gonadal ridge forms ovaries or testes rather than the ductal structures connecting the female reproductive organs.
notes.E: Mesonephric ducts form male internal genital ducts and generally regress in females rather than producing the Müllerian tract.

questions.stem: Virilisation of the mesonephric ducts into male genital ducts is driven by
questions.why: Testosterone produced by fetal Leydig cells promotes survival and differentiation of mesonephric ducts into the male internal reproductive tract. Dihydrotestosterone has a particularly important separate role in masculinisation of external genitalia and prostate.

notes.A: Dihydrotestosterone is especially important for external genital and prostatic development, rather than maintaining the mesonephric ducts themselves.
notes.B: Anti-Müllerian hormone causes paramesonephric duct regression, rather than directly promoting differentiation of the mesonephric ducts.
notes.C: Oestrogen is not the principal androgen-dependent signal maintaining male mesonephric duct differentiation during fetal development.
notes.D: SRY initiates testicular differentiation upstream, while testosterone is the direct endocrine signal supporting mesonephric duct development.

questions.stem: In the male, the paramesonephric ducts regress, leaving the appendix of the testis and the
questions.why: Mullerian remnants in the male are the appendix of the testis and the prostatic utricle.

questions.stem: A remnant of the mesonephric duct persisting in the wall of the female genital tract is
questions.why: The mesonephric duct may persist in the female as Gartner's duct/cyst alongside the vagina.

questions.stem: The lower one-third of the vagina is derived from the
questions.why: The upper vagina forms from the paramesonephric ducts; the lower part forms from the sinovaginal bulbs/vaginal plate of the urogenital sinus.

questions.stem: The broad ligament of the uterus is formed as the fusing paramesonephric ducts drag a fold of
questions.why: The midline fusion of the paramesonephric ducts pulls a transverse peritoneal fold across the pelvis, forming the broad ligament.

questions.stem: Complete failure of fusion of the paramesonephric ducts produces a
questions.why: Total non-fusion gives a double uterus and often double vagina (uterus didelphys).

questions.stem: Persistence of the midline septum between the fused paramesonephric ducts gives a
questions.why: Failure to resorb the median septum after fusion leaves a septate uterus.

questions.stem: The external genitalia develop from primordia that are indifferent until about week
questions.why: The external genitalia arise from common primordia and remain indifferent until about week 12.

questions.stem: The genital tubercle gives rise to the glans penis in the male and the
questions.why: The genital tubercle becomes the glans of the penis in males and the clitoris in females.

questions.stem: The labioscrotal (genital) swellings form the scrotum in the male and the
questions.why: Labioscrotal swellings fuse to form the scrotum in males and remain separate as the labia majora in females.

questions.stem: The urethral folds form the labia minora in the female and, in the male, the
questions.why: The urethral folds fuse over the urethral groove to form the penile urethra in males and remain as labia minora in females.

questions.stem: Differentiation of the male EXTERNAL genitalia depends specifically on
questions.why: DHT (from testosterone via 5-alpha-reductase) drives masculinisation of the external genitalia; the internal ducts need testosterone itself.

questions.stem: Hypospadias, in which the urethra opens on the ventral surface of the penis, results from failure of fusion of the
questions.why: Incomplete fusion of the urethral folds leaves the urethral opening on the underside of the penis.

questions.stem: The fibromuscular cord that guides descent of the gonad to the scrotum or labia is the
questions.why: The gubernaculum extends from the lower pole of the gonad to the labioscrotal swelling and guides its descent.

questions.stem: Indirect inguinal hernias are commoner on the right side because

options.label: B
options.text: the gubernaculum is longer on the right

options.label: C
options.text: the processus closes first on the left

questions.why: The left testis descends slightly earlier, so the right processus vaginalis tends to remain patent a little longer.

questions.stem: The tunica vaginalis covering the testis is derived from the
questions.why: The tunica vaginalis is formed from the processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum.

questions.stem: As the testis descends it acquires the internal spermatic fascia from the
questions.why: Internal spermatic fascia comes from transversalis fascia, cremasteric from internal oblique and external spermatic from external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.stem: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism), if bilateral and untreated, leads to
questions.why: Higher intra-abdominal temperature destroys spermatogonia, so bilateral cryptorchidism causes infertility; Leydig cells are spared.

questions.stem: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 46,XX fetus causes virilisation because of

options.label: D
options.text: a defect in the androgen receptor

questions.why: A 21-hydroxylase deficiency shunts adrenal steroids into androgens, masculinising the external genitalia of a genetic female.

questions.stem: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY) the external genitalia are female because
questions.why: Testes and testosterone are present, but target cells cannot respond to androgens, so external genitalia develop along the female pattern.

questions.stem: A 46,XY individual with female-appearing genitalia at birth who virilises at puberty ('guevedoces') typically has
questions.why: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency gives low DHT (female-type external genitalia at birth) but rising testosterone virilises them at puberty.

questions.stem: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, the uterus and uterine tubes are absent because
questions.why: Functioning Sertoli cells secrete AMH, so the Mullerian ducts regress even though the ducts cannot respond to androgens.

questions.stem: The central nervous system develops from the
questions.why: The CNS arises from the neural plate, a thickening of ectoderm (neuroectoderm) that appears in week 3.

questions.stem: The process by which the neural plate folds and closes into the neural tube is
questions.why: Neurulation is the folding of the neural plate into the neural tube.

questions.stem: Formation of the neural plate is induced by signals from the notochord and
questions.why: The notochord and paraxial mesoderm release factors that induce overlying ectoderm to become neural plate.

questions.stem: Besides the neural tube, neurulation also gives rise to the surface epidermis and the
questions.why: Ectoderm forms the neural tube, the neural crest and the epidermis of the skin.

questions.stem: The forebrain and midbrain are induced in ectoderm where BMP4 is inhibited by
questions.why: Noggin, chordin and follistatin inhibit BMP4 to permit forebrain-midbrain fate; WNT3a/FGF/retinoic acid permit hindbrain-spinal cord fate.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a derivative of neural crest cells?
questions.why: Neural crest forms melanocytes, sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla and much craniofacial tissue; limb muscle is from somites.

questions.stem: The adrenal (suprarenal) medulla is derived from
questions.why: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are neural crest derivatives; the cortex is from mesoderm.

questions.stem: The anterior (rostral) neuropore normally closes at about day
questions.why: The anterior neuropore closes around day 25-26; the posterior neuropore closes about two days later.

questions.stem: Failure of the anterior neuropore to close results in
questions.why: Non-closure of the anterior neuropore gives anencephaly; non-closure of the posterior neuropore gives spina bifida.

questions.stem: Failure of the posterior (caudal) neuropore to close results in
questions.why: Non-closure of the posterior neuropore gives spina bifida, with defective vertebral arches.

questions.stem: Maternal deficiency of which vitamin is strongly associated with neural tube defects?
questions.why: Folate (vitamin B9) deficiency increases the risk of neural tube defects, so periconceptional supplementation is advised.

questions.stem: The three primary brain vesicles, from cranial to caudal, are the prosencephalon, mesencephalon and
questions.why: The three primary vesicles are the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain) and rhombencephalon (hindbrain).

questions.stem: The cerebral hemispheres develop from the
questions.why: The prosencephalon forms the telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres) and the diencephalon (thalamus and optic vesicles).

questions.stem: The optic vesicles grow out from the
questions.why: The diencephalon gives rise to the optic vesicles as well as the thalamus and hypothalamus.

questions.stem: The cerebellum and pons develop from the
questions.why: The rhombencephalon forms the metencephalon (pons and cerebellum) and the myelencephalon (medulla).

questions.stem: The medulla oblongata develops from the
questions.why: The myelencephalon becomes the medulla oblongata, continuous with the spinal cord.

questions.stem: In the developing spinal cord the mantle layer becomes the
questions.why: The mantle layer (neuronal cell bodies) becomes grey matter; the outer marginal layer becomes white matter.

questions.stem: The motor neurons of the spinal cord develop in the
questions.why: The ventral basal plates form motor (efferent) neurons; the dorsal alar plates form sensory (afferent) neurons.

questions.stem: The sensory association neurons of the spinal cord develop in the
questions.why: The alar plates (dorsal) form sensory neurons; the basal plates (ventral) form motor neurons, separated by the sulcus limitans.

questions.stem: Which neuroglial cell type is NOT derived from neuroectoderm?
questions.why: Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ependyma arise from neuroectoderm; microglia come from mesenchyme (monocyte lineage).

questions.stem: In the adult the spinal cord typically ends at the level of
questions.why: Differential growth means the cord ends at about L3 at birth and L1 in the adult.

questions.stem: The oblique nerve roots and filum terminale at the lower end of the vertebral canal form the
questions.why: Below the conus the lumbosacral roots and filum terminale form the cauda equina.

questions.stem: Myelination of axons in the central nervous system is carried out by
questions.why: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons.

questions.stem: Which process of brain development removes under-used synaptic connections?
questions.why: Pruning weeds out underused connections and strengthens frequently used ones, mostly between about ages 3 and 16.

questions.stem: The limb buds first appear during week
questions.why: Limb buds appear on the ventrolateral body wall in week 4; forelimb buds appear slightly before hindlimb buds.

questions.stem: The core of each limb bud is formed from
questions.why: Somatic lateral plate mesoderm forms the limb bud core (bones and connective tissue); muscle comes later from somites.

questions.stem: Outgrowth of the limb bud is initiated by which signalling molecule from the lateral plate mesoderm?
questions.why: FGF10 from the lateral plate mesoderm triggers limb bud outgrowth.

questions.stem: The thickened ectoderm at the tip of the limb bud is the
questions.why: The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) caps the bud and controls proximo-distal outgrowth via FGF8.

questions.stem: The apical ectodermal ridge controls patterning along which axis?
questions.why: The AER drives proximo-distal patterning (shoulder to fingertip); the ZPA controls antero-posterior patterning.

questions.stem: The zone of polarising activity determines digit identity by secreting
questions.why: The ZPA at the posterior margin secretes SHH, which patterns the antero-posterior (thumb to little-finger) axis.

questions.stem: Dorsal identity of the limb (back of the hand) is specified by
questions.why: Wnt7a from dorsal ectoderm specifies dorsal fate; Engrailed-1 from ventral ectoderm specifies ventral fate.

questions.stem: From proximal to distal, the limb skeleton forms in the order stylopod, zeugopod and
questions.why: Stylopod (humerus/femur), then zeugopod (radius-ulna/tibia-fibula), then autopod (hand/foot).

questions.stem: The humerus and femur correspond to which limb segment?
questions.why: The stylopod is the proximal segment (humerus in the arm, femur in the leg).

questions.stem: Positioning of the limbs along the cranio-caudal axis is governed by
questions.why: HOX (homeobox) genes set the cranio-caudal position at which limbs form.

questions.stem: Forelimb (versus hindlimb) identity is specified by which transcription factor?
questions.why: TBX5 (with FGF10) specifies the forelimb; TBX4 (with FGF10) specifies the hindlimb.

questions.stem: By week 6 the flattened ends of the limb buds are called
questions.why: The limb buds flatten into hand and foot plates by week 6.

questions.stem: Separation of the digits occurs by
questions.why: Programmed cell death (apoptosis) removes the interdigital mesenchyme, freeing the fingers and toes.

questions.stem: The muscles of the limbs are derived from
questions.why: Myogenic cells migrate into the limb bud from the somites; the bones form from somatic lateral plate mesoderm.

questions.stem: The bones of the limbs form by
questions.why: Mesenchyme forms hyaline cartilage models that are replaced by bone through endochondral ossification; ossification centres appear about week 12.

questions.stem: During week 7 the upper limbs rotate so that the thumb comes to lie
questions.why: The upper limbs rotate 90 degrees laterally (thumb lateral); the lower limbs rotate medially (big toe medial).

questions.stem: During week 7 the lower limbs rotate so that the great toe comes to lie
questions.why: The lower limbs rotate 90 degrees medially, placing the great toe medially and the extensors anteriorly.

questions.stem: The upper limb buds lie opposite which spinal segments?
questions.why: The upper limb buds lie opposite the lower five cervical and upper two thoracic segments (C5-T2).

questions.stem: Thalidomide causes limb defects mainly by
questions.why: Thalidomide inhibits angiogenesis in the developing limb, producing phocomelia and amelia.

questions.stem: Complete absence of a limb is termed
questions.why: Amelia is total absence of a limb; meromelia is partial absence; phocomelia is absence of proximal parts with the hand/foot attached near the trunk.

questions.stem: Fusion of adjacent digits is called
questions.why: Syndactyly is fusion of digits (failed interdigital apoptosis); polydactyly is extra digits.

questions.stem: Extra digits (supernumerary fingers or toes) is termed
questions.why: Polydactyly is the presence of extra digits.

questions.stem: At puberty, spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules is directly initiated by
questions.why: FSH acts on the Sertoli cells to initiate spermatogenesis, while testosterone (driven by LH) sustains it; the whole axis is switched on by hypothalamic GnRH.

questions.stem: Normal spermatogenesis requires a testicular temperature that is about
questions.why: The scrotum keeps the testes 2-3 °C cooler than the core, which is essential for sperm production; this is why an undescended (intra-abdominal) testis fails to make sperm.

questions.stem: The phase of spermatogenesis in which type A spermatogonia multiply by mitosis to generate primary spermatocytes is called
questions.why: Spermatocytogenesis is the initial mitotic phase (~16 days) that amplifies spermatogonia into primary spermatocytes; spermiogenesis is the later remodelling of spermatids into spermatozoa.

questions.stem: Which event is characteristic of spermiogenesis?

options.label: A
options.text: reduction of the chromosome number to haploid

options.label: D
options.text: shedding of excess cytoplasm as a residual body

options.label: E
options.text: duplication of DNA before the first division

questions.why: Spermiogenesis remodels a round spermatid into a spermatozoon — forming the acrosome and tail and shedding excess cytoplasm — with no further division; chromosome reduction and crossing over happen earlier, in meiosis.

questions.stem: The primary oocyte completes its first meiotic division

options.label: A
options.text: during the fifth month of fetal life

options.label: B
options.text: only at the moment of fertilization

options.label: E
options.text: just before ovulation, in response to the LH surge

questions.why: Arrested in prophase I since fetal life, the primary oocyte finishes meiosis I at the LH surge to give a secondary oocyte and the first polar body; meiosis II is completed only if fertilization occurs.

questions.stem: The ovulated secondary oocyte stays arrested at which stage unless it is fertilized?

options.label: A
options.text: metaphase of the second meiotic division

options.label: B
options.text: prophase of the first meiotic division

options.label: C
options.text: metaphase of the first meiotic division

options.label: D
options.text: anaphase of the second meiotic division

options.label: E
options.text: telophase of the first meiotic division

questions.why: The secondary oocyte is ovulated in metaphase II and only finishes the division, expelling the second polar body, if a sperm penetrates it.

questions.stem: The continual degeneration of ovarian follicles at every stage of development is termed
questions.why: Follicular atresia removes the great majority of follicles throughout life, so of the roughly two million present at birth only about 400 ever ovulate; luteolysis instead means regression of the corpus luteum.

questions.stem: Apart from spermatozoa, semen is formed mainly by secretions of the
questions.why: Most of the ejaculate volume is seminal-vesicle and prostatic fluid that nourishes and activates the sperm; the testis and epididymis supply the sperm themselves, not the bulk fluid.

questions.stem: A normal semen sample contains approximately how many spermatozoa per millilitre?
questions.why: Normal semen carries on the order of 100 million sperm per millilitre; fertility generally needs at least ~15 million/mL with adequate motility and morphology.

questions.stem: Capacitation of spermatozoa in the female genital tract chiefly involves

options.label: A
options.text: release of hyaluronidase from the acrosomal cap

options.label: B
options.text: fusion of the sperm head with the oocyte membrane

options.label: C
options.text: condensation of the sperm nucleus within the head

options.label: D
options.text: shedding of the sperm tail before penetration

options.label: E
options.text: removal of a glycoprotein coat from the sperm plasmalemma

questions.why: Capacitation strips a glycoprotein coat from the sperm plasmalemma, exposing receptors so the sperm can later undergo the acrosome reaction; it precedes and is distinct from acrosomal enzyme release.

questions.stem: After the acrosome reaction, penetration of the zona pellucida is mediated mainly by
questions.why: Acrosin, exposed on the inner acrosomal membrane, digests the zona pellucida; hyaluronidase instead disperses the corona radiata and cumulus cells earlier.

questions.stem: The slow block to polyspermy is produced by

options.label: A
options.text: rapid depolarisation of the oocyte plasma membrane

options.label: B
options.text: release of cortical granules that alter the zona pellucida

options.label: C
options.text: immediate hardening of the corona radiata

options.label: D
options.text: closure of binding sites on the sperm tail

options.label: E
options.text: contraction of the oviduct around the oocyte

questions.why: Cortical granules discharged on sperm contact modify the zona (the zona reaction), making it impermeable to further sperm — the slow block to polyspermy.

questions.stem: The genetic sex of the zygote is determined by

options.label: A
options.text: whether the oocyte carries an X or a Y chromosome

options.label: B
options.text: the number of polar bodies the oocyte expels

options.label: C
options.text: whether the fertilizing sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome

options.label: D
options.text: the timing of ovulation relative to coitus

options.label: E
options.text: the level of testosterone in the semen

questions.why: The oocyte always carries an X, so the sperm’s sex chromosome — X (female) or Y (male) — sets the zygote’s genetic sex.

questions.stem: Entry of the spermatozoon triggers the secondary oocyte to

options.label: A
options.text: begin its first meiotic division from the start

options.label: B
options.text: expel the first polar body instead

options.label: D
options.text: complete meiosis II and expel the second polar body

options.label: E
options.text: duplicate all its chromosomes once more

questions.why: Sperm penetration releases the metaphase-II arrest, so the oocyte finishes meiosis II and extrudes the second polar body, leaving the haploid female pronucleus.

questions.stem: After ovulation, the secondary oocyte remains capable of being fertilized for about
questions.why: The ovulated oocyte is viable for roughly 24 hours; if no sperm reaches it in that window it degenerates and is shed with menstruation.

questions.stem: Within the female genital tract, spermatozoa may survive for up to about
questions.why: Sperm can survive up to roughly three days awaiting ovulation, so intercourse a few days before ovulation can still achieve fertilization.

questions.stem: In vivo, fertilization normally takes place in the
questions.why: Sperm and oocyte usually meet in the ampulla, the widest part of the uterine tube; the zygote then cleaves as it travels to the uterus for implantation.

questions.stem: Virtually all the cytoplasm and organelles of the zygote are contributed by the
questions.why: The large oocyte supplies essentially all the cytoplasm, mitochondria and organelles; the sperm contributes little more than its haploid nucleus and a centriole.

questions.stem: During cleavage the blastomeres stay enclosed within the zona pellucida, which prevents

options.label: C
options.text: compaction of the morula from occurring

options.label: E
options.text: attachment of the embryo to the oviduct

questions.why: The intact zona holds the blastomeres together, preventing premature implantation in the tube and premature separation into identical twins until the blastocyst hatches.

questions.stem: A solid ball of about 16 blastomeres formed during cleavage is called the
questions.why: At roughly the 16-cell stage the compacted ball of blastomeres is the morula; a fluid-filled cavity later converts it into a blastocyst.

questions.stem: A fluid-filled cavity first appears in the conceptus, forming the blastocyst, at about
questions.why: The blastocoel appears around day 5 as trophoblast cells pump fluid into the morula; the blastocyst then hatches from the zona and implants.

questions.stem: The secretory (receptive) endometrium needed for implantation is produced mainly under the influence of
questions.why: The corpus luteum, stimulated by LH, secretes progesterone that converts the proliferative endometrium into the receptive secretory phase.

questions.stem: Slight bleeding that sometimes accompanies implantation results from

options.label: A
options.text: shedding of the entire uterine lining

options.label: B
options.text: rupture of the corpus luteum cyst

options.label: C
options.text: detachment of the cervical mucus plug

questions.why: As the invading trophoblast digests endometrial tissue it erodes small maternal vessels, which can cause light implantation (false) bleeding.

questions.stem: After implantation, the part of the decidua lying between the conceptus and the myometrium is the
questions.why: The decidua basalis lies deep to the conceptus toward the myometrium and forms the maternal part of the placenta; the capsularis overlies it toward the uterine cavity.

questions.stem: Implantation at any site outside the body of the uterus is termed
questions.why: Ectopic implantation (most often tubal) occurs outside the uterine body; tubal sites are dangerous because rupture causes severe internal bleeding.

questions.stem: Dizygotic (fraternal) twins always have which membrane arrangement?

options.label: E
options.text: a single shared placenta and sac

questions.why: Arising from two separately implanting zygotes, dizygotic twins always have two chorions and two amnions (Di-Di).

questions.stem: Monozygotic twins that share a single (monochorionic) placenta are at particular risk of
questions.why: A shared placenta allows unbalanced blood flow between the twins through placental vascular anastomoses, causing twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

questions.stem: Conjoined twinning results from incomplete splitting that occurs after formation of
questions.why: Splitting after the bilaminar disc has formed (once organ progenitors have differentiated) is incomplete, producing conjoined twins; this is possible only in Mo-Mo twins.

questions.stem: The notochordal process grows forward (cranially) from

options.label: B
options.text: the prochordal plate at the cranial end

questions.why: The notochordal process extends cranially from the primitive (Hensen’s) node at the cranial end of the streak, laying down the embryonic midline.

questions.stem: Epiblast cells that never migrate through the primitive streak remain on the surface as the
questions.why: Once the ingressing cells have formed endoderm and mesoderm, the epiblast cells left on the surface become ectoderm, which forms the nervous system and epidermis.

questions.stem: All three primary germ layers of the embryo are derived from the
questions.why: During gastrulation the epiblast generates ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm; the hypoblast is displaced and contributes only to extraembryonic structures.

questions.stem: The paraxial mesoderm, lying on either side of the notochord, differentiates into
questions.why: Paraxial mesoderm segments into somites, which give rise to the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle and dermis.

questions.stem: The intermediate mesoderm gives rise mainly to the
questions.why: Intermediate mesoderm forms the urogenital system — the kidneys and the gonads; the heart and body wall arise from lateral plate mesoderm.

questions.stem: Along the length of the embryo, the somites are added in which sequence?
questions.why: Somites appear in a strict craniocaudal sequence from about days 20-31, which is why somite number is used to age young embryos.

questions.stem: In the adult, the only persisting remnant of the notochord is the

options.label: A
options.text: anterior longitudinal ligament of the spine

options.label: B
options.text: nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc

options.label: D
options.text: denticulate ligament of the spinal cord

options.label: E
options.text: filum terminale of the spinal cord

questions.why: The notochord largely regresses; its sole adult remnant is the nucleus pulposus at the centre of each intervertebral disc.

questions.stem: By inhibiting BMP signalling, the notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the
questions.why: The notochord (through SHH and BMP inhibition) induces the overlying ectoderm to become neuroectoderm — the neural plate that folds into the neural tube.

questions.stem: The bilaminar embryonic disc is composed of
questions.why: Before gastrulation the inner cell mass forms a bilaminar disc of epiblast (columnar, future embryo) and hypoblast (cuboidal); gastrulation then makes it trilaminar.

questions.stem: Ingression of epiblast cells at the primitive streak (EMT) requires loss of adhesion through repression of
questions.why: At the streak, Snail represses E-cadherin so epiblast cells lose epithelial adhesion and migrate inward as mesenchyme (epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition).
